📚 Reference Links

  • Normative definitions (proxy vs gateway) — RFC 9110 §3.7: Intermediaries

  • How a forward proxy tunnels TLS — RFC 9110 §9.3.6: CONNECT

  • Reverse proxy, the mental model — Cloudflare Learning: What is a reverse proxy?

  • Bonus — blog.cloudflare.com: A Primer on Proxies

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Read the topic name, cover the right column, self-test before reading the rest.

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Which side configures each? Forward: the client is configured to use it. Reverse: the client knows nothing, DNS points at it.
What does RFC 9110 call a reverse proxy? A gateway — "a proxy that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection".
How does a forward proxy handle HTTPS it can't decrypt? CONNECT host:443 — it becomes a blind TCP tunnel, seeing only SNI and byte counts.
Which one hides whom? Forward hides the client from the server. Reverse hides the servers from the client.
Which header carries the real client IP through a reverse proxy? X-Forwarded-For (or the standardised Forwarded); trust it only from hops you control.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Both sit in the middle of an HTTP conversation, but they face opposite directions and are owned by opposite parties. A forward proxy is configured by the client and speaks on the client's behalf — egress control, allow-listing, caching, anonymity. A reverse proxy is deployed by the service and pretends to be the origin — DNS points at it, and it terminates TLS, routes, and fans out to backends. RFC 9110 actually calls the second one a gateway. The interesting part is that the same binary — nginx, Envoy — does both, so the direction is a config decision, not a product.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

If both are nginx, what actually differs on the wire?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the request line and the trust direction change, or whether "proxy" is one undifferentiated word to you.

The request line differs. A client talking to a forward proxy sends the absolute URI — GET http://example.com/path HTTP/1.1 — because the proxy has to be told which origin to reach; the client deliberately addressed the proxy, so the destination cannot live only in the Host header. A client talking to a reverse proxy sends the ordinary origin form — GET /path HTTP/1.1 with Host: example.com — because as far as that client is concerned it is talking to example.com. That single difference is the cleanest tell.

For HTTPS the forward proxy path changes again: the client cannot send an absolute URI it hasn't encrypted yet, so it issues CONNECT example.com:443, the proxy opens a TCP socket to that host, replies 200 Connection Established, and then shovels bytes in both directions without understanding them. It sees the SNI in the ClientHello, the destination IP, timing and volume — and nothing else — unless you deploy a trusted CA on every client and let it MITM, which is what corporate TLS inspection is.

The trust direction inverts too. A reverse proxy is the first thing an untrusted request touches — everything upstream of it is hostile, everything downstream is yours — which is why it owns TLS termination, WAF, rate limiting and the X-Forwarded-For rewrite. A forward proxy is the last thing a trusted request touches on its way out, so the hostility is on the far side, and it owns allow-lists, DLP and egress logging.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

An LLM agent in your cluster needs to call arbitrary tool APIs. Forward proxy, or per-service egress rules?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard agent-security question once a product ships tool-calling; also arrives as "how do you stop the model from exfiltrating data?"

🎯 Really testing: whether you reach for the layer that can see hostnames, or settle for the layer that only sees IPs.

Security groups and NACLs match on IP and port. Modern SaaS sits behind CDN IP ranges that rotate and are shared across every tenant of that CDN, so an IP allow-list either blocks a vendor's next deploy or admits every other customer on the same edge. A forward proxy matches on hostname — "this agent may reach api.stripe.com and nothing else" is expressible there and nowhere below it.

The cost is that you have just put a mandatory, stateful hop in front of every outbound call. It needs to be HA, its connection pool becomes a capacity limit, and its timeouts stack on top of the ones the client already has. Agent traffic makes this worse than normal service traffic: calls are bursty, concurrency is high, and some are long-lived streams that a default 60-second idle timeout will cut mid-response.

My tipping point is whether the destination set is known and small. Three fixed vendor endpoints with stable IPs — security groups and a NAT gateway are the honest answer, and a proxy is over-engineering. An agent that can be pointed at whatever a tool registry contains — a forward proxy with an explicit allow-list is the only control that means anything, and the egress log it produces is the artifact your security review will actually ask for.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

5,000 pods behind one egress proxy. What runs out first?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up whenever someone proposes a centralised egress tier.

Ephemeral ports on the proxy's outbound side, well before CPU. Every proxied connection consumes one source port per (dest IP, dest port) tuple, out of Linux's default net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range of 32768–60999 — roughly 28,000 — and TIME_WAIT holds each for 2×MSL, commonly 60 seconds on Linux. If a popular destination resolves to a single IP, the ceiling is ~28k connections per minute to that one host, no matter how many cores you have. File descriptors go next, then the connection-tracking table if the proxy sits behind a NAT gateway.

It presents as latency, not errors, which is why it fools people. Connect time starts queueing, p99 climbs while p50 stays flat, and the application-side symptom is "the tool API got slow" — pointing everyone at the vendor. The signals that name it correctly are ss -s showing a wall of TIME_WAIT, "cannot assign requested address" in the proxy log, and connect-time metrics diverging from upstream response-time metrics. The fixes, in order: upstream keepalive pooling so you stop opening a connection per request; more proxy source IPs, since the range is per-IP; then widening the range and tcp_tw_reuse as the blunt instrument.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the network path for a multi-tenant AI product where users stream responses in and the model calls third-party tools out.

📍 Seen in the wild: the AI-platform framing of this section; the same shape as any live-conversation product that streams model output to a browser.

🎯 Really testing: whether you keep ingress and egress as separate tiers with separate policies, or blur them into "we have a proxy".

Start with the constraint that dominates: the ingress path carries long-lived streaming responses and the egress path carries short, high-fan-out tool calls. Those two traffic shapes want opposite tuning — the first wants long idle timeouts and no response buffering, the second wants aggressive timeouts and heavy connection reuse. One proxy tier tuned for both is tuned for neither, so they are two tiers.

Ingress: DNS → CDN/edge → L7 reverse proxy (ALB or Envoy) → gateway for auth and rate limiting → the streaming service. The reverse proxy terminates TLS, rewrites X-Forwarded-For, and — critically — has response buffering off for the SSE route, or the whole product streams in one lump at the end. Egress: service → forward proxy with a per-tenant hostname allow-list → NAT gateway → internet. The forward proxy is where per-tenant egress policy and the audit log live, because it is the only hop that sees hostnames.

The failure mode I would monitor first is the buffering one on ingress — it is silent, it passes every health check, and it only shows up as "time-to-first-token is 12 seconds" from users. Second is egress port exhaustion, watched as connect-time p99 on the forward proxy rather than as an error rate, because it degrades before it errors.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Dimension Forward proxy Reverse proxy (RFC: gateway)
Configured by The client (env vars, PAC file, transparent interception) The service owner; DNS points at it
Client awareness Client knows it exists and addresses it Client believes it is the origin
Request line Absolute URI, or CONNECT host:443 for TLS Origin form + Host header
Hides The client, from the server The servers, from the client
Owns Egress allow-lists, DLP, outbound caching, anonymity TLS termination, routing, LB, caching, WAF, compression
Sees on HTTPS SNI + IP + timing only, unless MITM with a trusted CA Everything — it holds the certificate
Scale limit hit first Ephemeral ports outbound Concurrent connections / file descriptors inbound
When you'd actually pick it You must control or audit what your workloads reach — agents, CI runners, regulated egress You must control how the world reaches you — every public service, always

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism is an exchange, not math: what changes is who is addressed, what the request line says, and which side holds the private key.

Stage by stage.

  1. Forward: client addresses the proxy deliberately. For plaintext HTTP it sends an absolute URI so the proxy knows the origin. For HTTPS it sends CONNECT, which costs one extra round trip before the TLS handshake even starts — the reason a forward proxy adds latency to every cold outbound call, not just the first.

  2. Forward: the tunnel is opaque. After 200 Connection Established the proxy relays bytes. Policy can therefore only be enforced on what is visible before encryption: the CONNECT target and the ClientHello's SNI. This is exactly why hostname allow-lists work and content inspection does not, absent a MITM CA.

  3. Reverse: DNS does the addressing. api.vendor.com resolves to the proxy's address. The client performs a completely ordinary TLS handshake — the certificate it validates belongs to the proxy, which is the whole point of TLS termination: the proxy can now read, route, cache and compress.

  4. Reverse: the hop is annotated, not hidden. Before forwarding, the proxy rewrites the connection-level truth into headers — X-Forwarded-For (original client IP), X-Forwarded-Proto (the client spoke TLS even though this hop is plaintext), X-Forwarded-Host. Backends that read the raw socket address instead see the proxy's IP, which is how rate limiting silently starts limiting the proxy rather than the users.

  5. Both: hop-by-hop headers do not survive. Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade are per-hop by RFC 9110; the proxy consumes and regenerates them. That is the mechanism behind "my WebSocket upgrade works locally and 400s behind the LB" — the Upgrade header was dropped because the proxy was not configured to pass it.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The reverse proxy is the single hop where you can change the behaviour of every request without deploying a service. Certificate rotation, a canary split, an emergency rate limit, a header fix for one broken client, a redirect for a retired path — each is a config change and a reload rather than a build-test-deploy cycle per service. That is why it exists even when there is one backend: the value is the control point, not the load spreading.

The observable it moves is error-rate composition and TTFB. A reverse proxy is where 502/503/504 are emitted, so its access log is the first place you learn whether a failure was "no healthy backend", "backend returned garbage" or "backend was too slow" — three different teams. And because it can buffer, it is where time-to-first-byte is either preserved or destroyed; on a streaming product that is the headline number users feel.

The forward proxy moves a different observable: what left the building. Without one, your egress record is flow logs — IP pairs and byte counts, which cannot answer "did this workload call an unapproved API". With one, the answer is a hostname per request: a compliance artifact, and increasingly an AI-safety one.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# --- REVERSE proxy: nginx is the origin as far as the client is concerned ---
server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  server_name api.example.com;          # DNS points here; we hold the cert

  location /v1/ {
    proxy_pass http://app_pool;         # upstream group, plaintext inside the VPC
    proxy_set_header Host $host;                        # preserve the client's Host
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # append, never overwrite
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;         # backend must know TLS happened
    proxy_http_version 1.1;             # 1.0 is the default here and kills keepalive + chunking
    proxy_read_timeout 60s;             # the timer that emits 504 when the app is slow
  }
}

# --- FORWARD proxy: the CLIENT is configured, the server is unaware ---
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://egress-proxy.internal:3128
curl -v https://api.vendor.com/v1/items   # curl issues CONNECT api.vendor.com:443 first

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Same two artifacts as Section 8, run for real: one request out through the egress proxy, one request in through nginx.

📥 curl https://api.vendor.com/v1/items   (HTTPS_PROXY set, cold)
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [1] CONNECT api.vendor.com:443 → proxy checks allow-list  ................ +1 RTT (~2ms in-VPC)
    │   200 Connection Established
    ▼
🔒 [2] TLS 1.3 handshake, client ↔ vendor, proxy relays bytes  ............... +1 RTT (~40ms)
    │   proxy log records: hostname, bytes, duration. Body: never seen.
    ▼
🎯 [3] 200 OK at t+~95ms — of which ~2ms is the tunnel setup the proxy added

📥 GET https://api.example.com/v1/items   (public client, cold)
    │
    ▼
🔒 [4] TLS 1.3 to nginx; nginx holds the cert  ............................... 2 RTT total setup
    │
    ▼
⚖️ [5] location /v1/ matches → proxy_pass http://app_pool
    │   X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9        (was empty, now the real client)
    │   X-Forwarded-Proto: https            (this hop is plaintext; backend must be told)
    │   Host: api.example.com               (preserved, or routing breaks in the app)
    ▼
⚙️ [6] pooled keepalive conn to app  ........................................ 0 RTT added
    │   proxy_read_timeout 60s armed here
    ▼
✅ [7] 200 OK back to client — Server: nginx, backend identity never exposed

  1. The CONNECT is a real round trip. In-VPC it is ~2ms and invisible; if your egress proxy lives in another region it is 40–80ms added to every outbound call, which is why centralised egress tiers are placed per-region, not globally.

  2. The proxy's log line is the entire security value. It holds api.vendor.com, the byte counts and the duration. It does not hold the request body, because after step 1 the proxy is relaying ciphertext. Any design that promises payload inspection here is quietly promising a MITM CA on every workload.

  3. proxy_http_version 1.1 is not optional. nginx defaults proxy_pass to HTTP/1.0 upstream, which disables keepalive to the backend and breaks chunked responses — so a streaming endpoint that works when you curl the app directly stalls when you curl it through nginx. This single default is behind a large share of "it works locally" streaming bugs.

  4. $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for appends; a bare $remote_addr overwrites. Overwriting is fine at the outermost hop and wrong at every inner one — it erases the client when there is a CDN in front. Whichever you choose, the backend must only trust the header from hops you control, or a client can simply send its own X-Forwarded-For and defeat your rate limiter.

  5. proxy_read_timeout is the 504 timer. It measures the gap between reads from the upstream, not total response time — which is why a slow-but-steady stream survives it and a stalled-then-fast one does not.

10. When TO Use This

  • Reverse proxy — whenever anything untrusted reaches your service, which is always. Even a single backend benefits: you get TLS termination and rotation in one place, a stable public identity while backends come and go, and the ability to change routing without a deploy.

  • Reverse proxy — when you need to change behaviour faster than you can ship. An emergency rate limit on one abusive path, a header fix for a client you cannot update, a redirect for a retired API version. Config-and-reload beats build-and-deploy under incident pressure.

  • Forward proxy — when the question "what did our workloads call?" must have an answer at hostname granularity. Regulated egress, CI runners that execute untrusted code, and above all agent tool-calling, where the set of reachable destinations is dynamic by design.

  • Forward proxy — when one place should hold the vendor credential. A shared forward proxy can inject the upstream API key so no individual service ever holds it.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not add a forward proxy when your egress set is small and static. Three known vendor endpoints behind a NAT gateway with security-group rules is simpler, has no extra hop, no extra failure domain, and no extra timeout to tune. A proxy earns its place when the destination list is dynamic — otherwise you have bought an outage source in exchange for a log you could have gotten from flow logs.

  • Do not put a buffering reverse proxy in front of a streaming path without changing its defaults. nginx buffers upstream responses by default and ALB/CloudFront have their own behaviours; the degradation is not an error but a silent collapse of time-to-first-token from 200ms to the full response duration. Every health check passes while the product feels broken. (See Item 121 — this is the section's most-hit production bug.)

  • Do not use a shared forward proxy for long-lived streams. Idle timeouts on a shared egress tier are tuned for short RPCs; a 10-minute model response or a WebSocket to a vendor will be cut mid-flight, and the client sees a truncated body rather than a clean error.

  • Do not reverse-proxy when the protocol is not HTTP and you gain nothing from L7. Terminating and re-originating a raw TCP protocol at L7 costs you visibility you cannot use and adds a hop; an L4 pass-through is both faster and more honest. (Item 106.)

  • Scale limit to name out loud: a reverse proxy tier is bounded by concurrent connections and file descriptors long before CPU on streaming workloads, and a forward proxy tier by ephemeral ports outbound. Neither is a "just add cores" problem.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A reverse proxy and a load balancer are two different things."

✅ Reality: Load balancing is one responsibility a reverse proxy can hold, alongside TLS termination, routing, caching and compression. nginx, Envoy and HAProxy are all reverse proxies that happen to balance. The distinction that matters is L4 versus L7 (Item 108), not "proxy versus balancer".

❌ Misconception: "A forward proxy can inspect and filter HTTPS traffic."

✅ Reality: After CONNECT it relays ciphertext. It sees the SNI, the destination, the timing and the byte counts — enough for hostname policy, nothing like content filtering. Payload inspection requires terminating TLS with a CA you have installed on every client, which is a materially different security and privacy decision.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The X-Forwarded-For header tells me who the client is."

✅ Reality: It tells you what the previous hop chose to write, and any client can send one. It is only trustworthy from the outermost hop inward, and only when every hop in between is yours and appends rather than overwrites. Rate limiters and audit logs built on an unvalidated X-Forwarded-For are trivially spoofable.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Answering "it's a middleman" and stopping. Both are middlemen; the whole question is which party deployed it and which party it hides. Lead with ownership and direction — client-configured versus DNS-addressed — and the rest follows without you reciting a feature list.

Forgetting that the reverse proxy is the thing emitting your 5xx. When asked to debug a 502, a shallow answer says "the backend is down". The precise answer is that the proxy produced that status: 502 means it got an unusable response, 503 that it had nowhere healthy to send, 504 that it gave up waiting. Naming the emitter is what shows you have actually read a proxy log.

Talking about the client and the origin as if nothing is in between. Most production bugs here live in the middle — a dropped Upgrade header, an overwritten X-Forwarded-For, an HTTP/1.0 upstream default, a buffered stream. An answer that never mentions what the hop rewrote describes a diagram, not a system.

Claiming latency numbers without saying where the time goes. "A proxy adds a bit of latency" is a non-answer. The defensible version: a forward proxy adds one CONNECT round trip on cold connections plus the distance to the proxy; a reverse proxy adds a decrypt hop but usually saves round trips by holding a warm upstream pool.

Stopping at the happy path. No answer for what happens when the proxy itself is unhealthy. A centralised egress tier is a hard dependency for every outbound call in the estate — if you propose one and cannot say how it fails and what its blast radius is, you have proposed a single point of failure with a nice log file.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Forward proxy adds a CONNECT RTT plus distance to the proxy on every cold call; reverse proxy adds a decrypt hop but usually nets negative by holding warm upstream pools
💰 Cost A reverse proxy tier is cheap and shared; a centralised egress tier is a per-GB data-processing line item stacked on top of NAT gateway charges
🔒 Security / visibility Reverse proxy sees everything because it holds the key — that is the feature and the blast radius; forward proxy sees only hostnames unless you MITM every client
📈 Scale Both are connection-bound, not CPU-bound: file descriptors inbound, ephemeral ports outbound. Streaming workloads hit this an order of magnitude earlier than request/response ones
🔧 Ops complexity Every proxy is another config surface with its own timeout hierarchy; mismatched timeouts between hops are the most common self-inflicted 504
🐛 Debuggability The proxy log is the best single source of truth in the path — and the reason curl against the app succeeds while the browser fails, because you skipped the hop that rewrites headers

16. Real World Usage

Corporate and CI egress control. Self-hosted CI runners and anything executing third-party code are routinely placed behind a forward proxy with a package-registry allow-list, because a dependency's post-install script is untrusted code with network access. The proxy log turns "we ran their code" into "we know what their code called".

Agent tool-calling. The current wave of this pattern: an LLM agent's egress runs through a forward proxy holding a per-tenant hostname allow-list, because the destination set is chosen by a model at runtime and no static IP rule can express the policy. This is the same control the index delegates to Section 16's agent-egress item — the mechanism is here, the AI-specific policy lives there.

Every CDN is a reverse proxy. Cloudflare, Fastly and CloudFront are reverse proxies at global scale: DNS points at them, they hold your certificate, they cache and they shield the origin. The 2021 Fastly outage — one customer config change triggering a latent bug that took a large fraction of the web's edge offline — is the public reminder that this tier is a shared failure domain, not just a convenience.

📚 Reference Links

  • Where each responsibility is configured — nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module

  • The full request path through a modern proxy — Envoy: Life of a Request

  • What an intermediary may and may not change — RFC 9110 §3.7: Intermediaries

  • Cache semantics the proxy must honour — RFC 9111: HTTP Caching

  • Bonus — cloudflare.com/learning: What is a reverse proxy?

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Six responsibilities, in path order? Terminate TLS → route → rate limit → cache → forward (rewrite headers) → compress/buffer the response.
Which headers must the proxy regenerate rather than forward? Hop-by-hop: Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade, TE, Proxy-Authenticate.
What does proxy_buffering on cost you? Time-to-first-byte on streaming responses — the client gets nothing until a buffer fills.
Who compresses, proxy or app? Compress once, at the proxy — and never compress an already-compressed or streaming body blindly.
What makes a proxy cache entry unique? The cache key: method + URI + whatever Vary names. A missing Vary is how one user gets another's page.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A reverse proxy is the one hop that owns everything a request needs before it becomes application logic. In order: it terminates TLS, matches a route, applies admission control, checks its cache, rewrites headers so the backend knows who the client really was, forwards over a pooled keepalive connection, then compresses and — by default — buffers the response on the way back. Six jobs, one config file, no deploy needed to change any of them. The one that bites is buffering: it is on by default in nginx, and it silently converts a token stream into a single late blob.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through what the proxy does to a request, in order.

🎯 Really testing: whether you hold an ordered pipeline or an unordered list of features — because the order is what determines what each stage can see.

The order is forced by visibility. TLS termination comes first, because until the bytes are decrypted the only thing available is the SNI; every subsequent decision needs the path, method and headers, so nothing else can run before it. Routing comes next — host and path matching against a rule table — because the chosen route carries the rest of the config: which upstream pool, which timeouts, which cache policy.

Admission control follows routing and precedes the cache lookup, because you want an abusive client rejected before it costs you a cache read, and because limits are usually per-route. Then the cache: a hit ends the request here and the backend never learns it happened, which is the entire point. On a miss, the proxy rewrites headers — appending X-Forwarded-For, setting X-Forwarded-Proto, stripping hop-by-hop fields — and forwards over a pooled upstream connection, so no TCP or TLS handshake is paid on the inside.

On the way back the pipeline runs in reverse: the response may be stored in the cache, compressed if the client advertised Accept-Encoding and the type is compressible, and buffered before delivery. Buffering last is why it is so easy to miss — every earlier stage behaved correctly.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Terminate TLS at the proxy, or pass it through to the backend?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard opener once someone says "reverse proxy"; the compliance version is "we were told encryption must be end-to-end".

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that L7 capability and end-to-end encryption are mutually exclusive at the same hop.

Terminating buys you everything L7: path routing, per-request load balancing, caching, compression, WAF inspection, header rewriting and readable access logs. Passing through buys you one thing — the backend holds the only key — and costs you all of the above, because a proxy that cannot read the request can only balance connections and match SNI. You cannot have both at one hop; that is not a tuning decision, it is arithmetic.

The usual resolution is terminate and re-encrypt: the proxy decrypts, does its work, and opens a second TLS session to the backend. You keep L7 capability and nothing crosses the network in plaintext, at the cost of a second handshake — amortised to near zero by a keepalive pool — and of the proxy being a genuine plaintext point in memory. For most regulated environments that satisfies "encrypted in transit"; where it does not, the requirement is usually really mTLS to the backend, which re-encryption also gives you.

I pass through only when the payload must be unreadable by infrastructure I operate — end-to-end encrypted messaging, a payment path under strict scope reduction — or when the protocol is not HTTP and L7 gives me nothing. Everywhere else, terminating and re-encrypting is the default, and the honest trade to state out loud is that the proxy becomes a high-value target holding a wildcard certificate.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

50,000 concurrent SSE streams through one nginx tier. What runs out?

📍 Seen in the wild: the capacity question behind every LLM streaming product.

File descriptors and worker connections, long before CPU. Each stream holds one client socket and one upstream socket open for its entire life, so 50k streams is ~100k descriptors on the proxy. nginx's worker_connections defaults to 512 per worker and the process ulimit -n is commonly 1024 unless raised — both must be lifted explicitly, and worker_connections × worker_processes must exceed twice your concurrent stream count. Memory is the second wall: with buffering on, each in-flight response reserves proxy_buffers — the default 8×4k or 8k — so 50k streams reserve gigabytes for data nobody wanted buffered.

It presents as a hard cliff rather than a gradient. Below the limit everything is fine; at the limit new connections are accepted by the kernel and then immediately dropped, so clients see connection resets while the proxy's CPU sits at 20% and every existing stream keeps working perfectly. nginx -V-level tuning aside, the diagnostic signals are worker_connections are not enough in the error log, accept() failures, and the listen backlog (ss -lnt Recv-Q at somaxconn) saturating. The fixes are raising the descriptor and worker-connection limits, turning buffering off for streaming routes so memory stops being reserved, and — past a point — horizontal scale, because a single proxy holding 100k long-lived sockets is a large blast radius regardless of whether it fits.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Where do you place these six responsibilities across CDN, ingress and gateway in a Kubernetes-hosted product?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that these are responsibilities that can be redistributed, not a monolith that must live in one box.

The dominant constraint is that each responsibility wants to be as close to the client as it can be without needing information it doesn't have. Static caching and DDoS absorption want the CDN edge, hundreds of PoPs away from your cluster, because they can be decided from the URL alone. TLS termination happens at least twice — once at the edge, once at the ingress — because the edge cannot forward a session it terminated. Per-tenant rate limiting wants the gateway, because it needs the identity that only auth produces.

Concretely: CDN holds TLS #1, static caching, WAF and bot mitigation. The Kubernetes ingress controller holds TLS #2, host/path routing to Services and the X-Forwarded-* rewrite. The API gateway behind it holds auth, quota, per-tenant limits and request transformation. Compression is set once, at the CDN, and disabled everywhere behind it so nothing is compressed twice. Buffering is off end-to-end on streaming routes and left on for everything else — three hops, three places to get that wrong.

The failure mode I would monitor first is header trust across those hops: X-Forwarded-For must append at every layer and be trusted only from the previous known hop, or the gateway's per-tenant limiter is limiting the ingress controller's IP for everyone. Second is cache-key correctness at the edge — a missing Vary: Authorization on a personalised route is how one tenant is served another tenant's response, and it is a data-leak class bug, not a performance one.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Responsibility Decided from Cheapest place to do it What goes wrong when misplaced
TLS termination SNI + certificate Closest hop that needs to read L7 Pass-through blinds routing, caching and WAF
Routing Host, path, headers Ingress / L7 proxy Routing in the app means a deploy to change a URL
Rate limiting Client identity Gateway (needs auth) At the edge it limits by IP and punishes NAT'd users
Caching Method + URI + Vary CDN edge for static; proxy for shared dynamic Missing Vary serves one user's response to another
Header rewriting Connection facts Every hop, appending Overwriting X-Forwarded-For erases the real client
Compression Accept-Encoding + content type Once, outermost hop Double compression, or compressing a stream and stalling it
Buffering Response shape Off for streams, on for uploads The silent TTFB killer on SSE and token streaming

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism is an ordered pipeline where each stage is gated on information produced by the previous one.

Stage notes.

  1. TLS termination costs 1 RTT on a cold TLS 1.3 connection and zero on a resumed one. Everything downstream depends on it: a proxy that has not decrypted can route on SNI and nothing else.

  2. Routing is a first-match rule table. nginx orders location blocks by prefix and regex precedence rather than file order — a fact that surprises people during incidents. A miss is answered by the proxy, which is why a 404 with Server: nginx and no application log line means "no route matched", not "the app rejected it".

  3. Admission control before cache means a rejected request costs one counter increment. Reversing them lets an abusive client farm cache reads for free.

  4. The cache key is the whole correctness story. RFC 9111 makes the key method + target URI, extended by whatever Vary names. A response that differs per user but does not say Vary: Authorization — or is not marked private — is eligible to be handed to the next requester. This is the one responsibility in the list where the failure is a data leak.

  5. Header rewriting separates connection truth from request truth. The backend's socket sees the proxy; the headers carry the client. Hop-by-hop fields (Connection, Keep-Alive, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade, TE) are per-connection by definition and must be consumed and regenerated — the reason a WebSocket Upgrade vanishes unless explicitly re-set.

  6. Forwarding on a pooled connection is where the latency is won back. A warm upstream pool means the inside hop costs no handshake at all, which is how a proxy that adds a decrypt step still ends up net faster than direct-to-backend for cold clients.

  7. The response stages are where streaming dies. Compression buffers by nature; nginx's proxy_buffering on default holds the response until a buffer fills or the upstream closes. Both are correct for a 200KB JSON document and catastrophic for a token stream.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This is the hop where the cost curve bends. A proxy cache in front of a dynamic endpoint with a 30-second TTL takes a 10,000 rps read path down to ~30 rps at the backend — a three-order-of-magnitude reduction that no amount of application optimisation matches. Compression at the proxy cuts egress bytes on JSON by 70–80%, which on a metered path is a line item, not a nicety.

The observable it moves most visibly is TTFB and its variance. Cache hits collapse it to edge latency; buffering inflates it to full-response latency; a warm upstream pool removes two handshakes from every cold client's first request. On a streaming product, TTFB is time-to-first-token, and it is the number users describe as "feels fast" or "feels broken".

It is also where incident response starts. The proxy access log holds status, upstream address, upstream response time and total time on every request — enough to separate "we were slow" from "the backend was slow" from "there was no backend" without instrumenting a single service.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

upstream app_pool {
  server 10.0.1.11:8080;
  server 10.0.1.12:8080;
  keepalive 64;                       # warm upstream pool: no TCP/TLS handshake per request
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  server_name api.example.com;        # 1. TLS terminated here

  gzip on;                            # 6. compress once, outermost hop only
  gzip_types application/json text/plain;

  location /v1/ {                     # 2. route match
    limit_req zone=perip burst=20 nodelay;            # 3. admission control, before cache
    proxy_cache api_cache;                            # 4. cache; key includes Vary
    proxy_cache_valid 200 30s;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;                                   # 5. header rewriting
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;   # append, never overwrite
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;           # required for keepalive + chunked upstream
    proxy_set_header Connection "";   # strip the hop-by-hop header so keepalive survives
    proxy_pass http://app_pool;
  }

  location /v1/stream {               # 7. the streaming exception
    proxy_pass http://app_pool;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_buffering off;              # OFF, or tokens arrive as one late blob
    gzip off;                         # compression re-buffers what we just unbuffered
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;         # a long stream is not an idle connection
  }
}

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Two requests against the config above: a cacheable read, then a stream.

📥 GET /v1/items      (cold client, 203.0.113.9)
    │
    ▼
🔒 [1] TLS 1.3 handshake terminated at nginx  ..................... 1 RTT, ~25ms
    │
    ▼
🚦 [2] location /v1/ matched → limit_req: 3 of 20 burst used  ..... +0.1ms
    │
    ▼
⚡ [3] proxy_cache lookup → HIT, age 12s of 30s  .................. +0.3ms
    │   X-Cache-Status: HIT ; backend never contacted
    ▼
📦 [4] gzip: 41KB JSON → 6.2KB  .................................. +1.1ms
    │
    ▼
🎯 [5] 200 OK, TTFB ~27ms — 25 of which was the handshake

📥 GET /v1/stream     (same client, connection reused)
    │
    ▼
⚙️ [6] location /v1/stream matched → buffering OFF, gzip OFF
    │
    ▼
🔗 [7] pooled upstream conn taken from keepalive 64  .............. 0 RTT added
    │   X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9   X-Forwarded-Proto: https
    │   Connection: ""  → hop-by-hop stripped, keepalive preserved
    ▼
⚙️ [8] app emits first SSE frame at t+180ms → forwarded immediately
    │   (with proxy_buffering on, this frame would have waited for 8x4k or EOF)
    ▼
✅ [9] client renders first token at ~181ms — TTFB equals app think-time, nothing added

  1. The cache hit is the whole performance story of request one. 0.3ms of proxy work replaced an application round trip and a database read. It also means the backend's request-rate graph under-reports real traffic by the hit ratio — a fact worth stating before someone sizes a fleet from it.

  2. limit_req ran before the cache lookup. Had the order been reversed, a client hammering a cached path would consume proxy I/O for free. Rate limiting is cheap only when it is early.

  3. gzip on the JSON path saved 85% of the bytes and cost about a millisecond. On the stream path it is explicitly off, because gzip's buffer would re-introduce exactly the latency proxy_buffering off just removed.

  4. proxy_set_header Connection "" is the non-obvious line. nginx sends Connection: close upstream by default; blanking it, together with proxy_http_version 1.1, is what actually keeps the upstream keepalive pool alive. Without both, the keepalive 64 directive is decorative and every request pays a fresh TCP handshake inside the VPC.

  5. The two location blocks differ in exactly the settings that matter for shape. Same upstream, same TLS, same headers — and opposite buffering, compression and timeout. That contrast is the note: a reverse proxy's responsibilities are per-route, and treating them as global is how one config serves one traffic shape well and the other badly.

10. When TO Use This

  • In front of every public HTTP service, without exception. Even a single backend gets TLS in one rotatable place, a stable public identity, and the ability to change routing without a deploy.

  • When one shared responsibility should not be re-implemented per service. Compression, access logging, X-Forwarded-* normalisation and TLS are cross-cutting; doing them once at the proxy is strictly less code and strictly more consistent than doing them in five languages.

  • When a read path is hot and slightly stale is acceptable. A 30-second proxy cache in front of a dynamic endpoint is the single highest-leverage change available for a read-heavy service.

  • When you need a control point during an incident. Shedding one abusive path, pinning traffic away from a bad AZ, or serving stale-while-revalidate during a backend outage are all proxy-config moves available in minutes.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not let the proxy cache anything personalised without proving the cache key. If the response varies by user, it needs Cache-Control: private or a Vary that names the varying header. Getting this wrong does not degrade — it leaks one user's data to another, and it will be found by a customer, not by a metric.

  • Do not terminate TLS at a proxy you do not trust with the plaintext. For end-to-end encrypted payloads, pass-through is the only correct answer, and you must then accept that routing, caching, WAF and readable logs are gone.

  • Do not leave the response-side defaults alone on a streaming route. Buffering on and compression on are correct for documents and wrong for streams; the failure is silent, passes health checks, and shows up only as user-perceived latency.

  • Do not push per-tenant rate limiting to a hop that has no identity. At the CDN edge the only key is IP, which over-limits NAT'd corporate users and under-limits a distributed abuser. That responsibility belongs behind auth.

  • Do not stack proxies without auditing the timeout hierarchy. CDN, ALB, ingress and gateway each have their own idle and read timeouts; when an inner timeout exceeds an outer one, the outer hop times out first and reports a 504 that names the wrong culprit.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The proxy just forwards the request."

✅ Reality: It rewrites it. Hop-by-hop headers are consumed and regenerated, X-Forwarded-* is added, the HTTP version to the upstream may differ from the client's, and the response may be compressed, cached and buffered. "Forwarded" describes the intent, not the bytes.

❌ Misconception: "Enabling gzip at the proxy is always a win."

✅ Reality: It costs CPU and, more importantly, it buffers. On an SSE or chunked stream, compression re-introduces the latency you disabled buffering to remove; and re-compressing already-compressed bodies (images, video, gzipped payloads) burns CPU for nothing.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "keepalive 64 in the upstream block means the proxy keeps upstream connections alive."

✅ Reality: Not on its own. nginx still speaks HTTP/1.0 upstream by default and still sends Connection: close. You need proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection "" alongside it. Until all three are present, every upstream request pays a fresh TCP handshake and the pool sits unused.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Listing the responsibilities without the ordering. "TLS, routing, caching, compression" as an unordered set invites the follow-up you cannot answer: why can't the cache come first? The order is forced by what each stage can see, and saying so is the difference between having read a feature list and having debugged one.

Treating configuration as global. Real proxies are configured per route, and the interesting cases are exactly where two routes need opposite settings on the same server block. If your answer has one buffering setting for the whole service, you have not met a streaming endpoint.

Ignoring the cache-key correctness dimension. Caching is usually discussed as a performance feature; at a proxy it is also a multi-tenancy hazard. Bringing up Vary and Cache-Control: private unprompted signals that you have owned a shared cache rather than only benefited from one.

Saying the proxy "adds latency" without netting it out. It adds a decrypt hop and subtracts a handshake, a DNS lookup and often an entire backend round trip. The honest answer is a small addition on warm paths and a large subtraction on cold and cached ones.

Having no answer for what the proxy does when the backend is gone. Serve stale, fail fast, queue, or shed? A reverse proxy's behaviour during a backend outage is a design decision, and "it returns 502" is the default, not the design.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
nginx proxy_buffering default on Must be off per-route for SSE and token streaming nginx ngx_http_proxy_module
nginx proxy_buffers default 8 × 4k or 8k page size Reserved per in-flight response; the memory wall at high concurrency nginx ngx_http_proxy_module
nginx proxy_read_timeout default 60 s Between upstream reads; fires as 504 nginx ngx_http_proxy_module
nginx upstream HTTP version default 1.0 Disables upstream keepalive and chunked responses until set to 1.1 nginx ngx_http_proxy_module
nginx worker_connections default 512 Total sockets per worker; a proxied request uses two nginx core module docs
gzip on typical JSON 70–85% size reduction The egress-cost lever; do it once, outermost Compression is content-dependent — measure yours

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency A decrypt hop is added; a handshake, a DNS lookup and often a whole backend round trip are removed. Buffering is the one setting that can make it strictly worse
💰 Cost Compression and caching are the two biggest egress and backend-fleet levers you have; the proxy tier itself is a rounding error beside what it saves
🔒 Security / visibility Terminating gives you WAF, logs and routing — and makes the proxy a wildcard-certificate-holding target with plaintext in memory
📈 Scale Bound by file descriptors and worker connections, not CPU. Long-lived streams hit this an order of magnitude earlier than request/response traffic
🔧 Ops complexity Per-route config multiplies: every new traffic shape is a new set of buffering, timeout and compression decisions across every hop in the chain
🐛 Debuggability The access log with upstream time and status is the best triage artifact in the path — and the reason curl against the app works while the browser fails, since curl skipped the hop that rewrites

16. Real World Usage

The ingress tier of essentially every Kubernetes platform. NGINX Ingress, Traefik and Envoy-based controllers are reverse proxies with the responsibility list above expressed as CRDs; annotations like nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off" exist precisely because the streaming exception is common enough to need a per-Ingress switch.

LLM API front doors. Every hosted model provider serves token streams through a reverse-proxy tier with buffering disabled and long read timeouts on the streaming route, and normal buffering on the non-streaming one. The two-location-block shape in Section 8 is not a teaching example; it is what the real config looks like.

Stale-while-revalidate as an outage shield. Large publishers configure their proxy tier to serve stale cached content while the origin is unreachable, which converts an origin outage into a staleness incident. It is the cheapest availability win in the list and it lives entirely in the proxy's cache configuration.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 104-forward-vs-reverse-proxy.md — which direction this note is about, and why the client is unaware

  • 07-http-semantics/62-http-caching.md — freshness, Vary and Cache-Control, which the proxy cache implements

  • 07-http-semantics/61-headers.md — hop-by-hop versus end-to-end, the rule behind header rewriting

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 108-l4-vs-l7.md — the decision of whether to have these responsibilities at all

  • 116-api-gateway.md — the responsibilities that need identity, split out into their own tier

  • 121-buffering-vs-streaming-proxies.md — the response-side default that this note flags twice

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • L4 pass-through — keep TLS end-to-end and give up every L7 responsibility (Item 106)

  • Service mesh sidecar — the same responsibilities per-pod instead of at a shared tier (Item 118)

  • In-application middleware — viable for one service, unmanageable across a fleet in three languages

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • CDN — takes caching, compression and WAF further out; this tier keeps routing and identity-aware work (Item 119)

  • Health checks — decide which upstreams the forward stage is allowed to choose (Item 112)

  • Load balancing algorithms — how the forward stage picks among healthy upstreams (Item 109)

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

The framing is usually "draw the path from a browser to your service and tell me what each box does." The answer that scores is not the box list but the responsibility assignment: which hop terminates TLS, where the cache key is computed, which hop knows the tenant, and where buffering is disabled. A senior reviewer will then move one responsibility to the wrong hop and ask what breaks — moving rate limiting to the edge, or caching a personalised route — and the discussion is really about whether you can predict the failure.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (5k concurrent streams) Worker connections and file descriptors on one proxy Raise worker_connections and ulimit -n; buffering off frees the reserved buffers
100× (50k streams) Memory for per-response buffers; single-proxy blast radius Horizontal proxy tier behind an L4 balancer; streaming routes isolated to their own pool
1000× (500k streams) Egress bytes and cross-AZ transfer dominate the bill; one region is a liability Multi-region proxy tiers with global routing; compression at the outermost hop only; cache aggressively at the edge to keep bytes off the origin path

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: buffering memory. Reserved proxy_buffers per in-flight response turns concurrency into gigabytes; the metric that moves first is proxy RSS, not latency.

  • 100×: connection ceilings. New connections are reset while existing ones are healthy and CPU is idle — a cliff, not a slope.

  • Operational: a config reload that changes a cache key or a Vary header. It deploys instantly, to everyone, with no canary, and the symptom is wrong data rather than errors.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Upstream response time versus total request time, per route. Divergence isolates proxy-side cost (queueing, buffering, compression) from application cost — the single most useful pair of numbers this tier produces.

  • Cache hit ratio per route, with an alert on a sudden drop. A collapse usually means a cache key changed and the backend is about to take the full unshielded load.

  • Active connections against the worker-connection ceiling, as a ratio. Alert at 70%, because the failure past 100% is a reset cliff rather than a gradual degradation.

  • X-Cache-Status distribution and 5xx composition (502 / 503 / 504 split). Three different causes, three different teams, one log field.

📚 Reference Links

  • The reference L4 balancer — AWS: Network Load Balancers

  • What an L4 health check can and cannot see — AWS: Health checks for NLB target groups

  • L4 proxying in nginx — nginx: ngx_stream_proxy_module

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does an L4 balancer decide on? The 5-tuple — src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port, protocol. Nothing above it.
Per what does it balance? Per connection, not per request. A connection is pinned for its whole life.
What does the backend see as the client IP? The real client IP if the balancer preserves it (NLB does); otherwise the balancer's.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An L4 load balancer picks a backend from the connection's 5-tuple and then gets out of the way — it does not parse HTTP, does not terminate TLS, and does not know what a request is. That buys enormous throughput and microsecond-scale added latency, and on AWS an NLB preserves the client's source IP so backends see the real address. The cost is that balancing is per connection, so one long-lived connection sends every request it carries to a single backend — which is exactly how gRPC and HTTP/2 traffic ends up unbalanced.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

How does an L4 balancer route a packet without reading the payload?

An L4 balancer hashes the connection's 5-tuple to select a target, then records that choice in a flow table so every subsequent packet of the same connection reaches the same backend. Nothing about the payload participates; the balancer could be carrying HTTP, Postgres wire protocol, MQTT or raw bytes and behave identically. That protocol-agnosticism is the defining property, not a side effect.

Two implementation styles matter. A proxying L4 balancer terminates the client TCP connection and opens its own to the backend, so it holds two sockets and can absorb slow clients. A pass-through balancer (NLB in its usual mode, and Linux IPVS) rewrites or encapsulates packets and lets the backend terminate the client's TCP connection directly — which is how the real source IP survives and how return traffic can bypass the balancer entirely under direct server return. The second is faster and gives you almost no visibility.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

When would you deliberately choose L4 over L7 for an HTTP service?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can name a reason other than "it's faster", which alone is rarely decisive.

Three reasons hold up. First, the payload must stay encrypted end-to-end — the backend holds the certificate and the balancer must not; L4 is then the only option, and every L7 feature is off the table by definition. Second, extreme connection volume with tiny per-connection cost, where the per-request parsing of an L7 tier is pure overhead and the flow-hash approach scales close to line rate. Third, the protocol is not HTTP at all — database connections, message brokers, game traffic — where L7 has nothing to offer.

The reason that does not hold up on its own is latency. An L7 hop typically adds a fraction of a millisecond within a datacentre, which is invisible next to a backend that thinks for 40ms. Choosing L4 to save that, and thereby giving up retries, path routing, per-request balancing and readable logs, is a bad trade for a normal HTTP service. The honest tipping point is: do I need the balancer to understand requests? If yes, L7; if the answer is genuinely no, L4 is simpler and cheaper.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Proxying L4 (nginx stream, HAProxy TCP mode) Pass-through L4 (NLB, IPVS)
Client IP at backend Balancer's, unless PROXY protocol is enabled Preserved natively
Connection termination At the balancer, two sockets At the backend, one socket
Slow-client absorption Yes No — the backend wears it
Added latency Sub-millisecond Near zero
When you'd actually pick it You want buffering and a single egress identity You want raw throughput and the real source IP

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The single decision point is the SYN. After it, the flow-table entry makes every later packet cheap — a lookup, not a hash — and makes every later request undirectable. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism: an L4 balancer's cost is O(connections) while its balancing quality is also O(connections), so traffic that carries many requests per connection is balanced exactly as badly as its connection distribution.

The math worth carrying: with n backends and c long-lived client connections, load skew follows the balls-in-bins distribution of c over n. At c = n the expected fraction of backends receiving zero connections is about 1/e ≈ 37% — over a third of the fleet idle while others carry two or three connections. Skew only becomes tolerable when c is an order of magnitude larger than n, which is precisely the condition that fails for a handful of gRPC clients (Item 114).

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not for HTTP/2 or gRPC between a small number of clients and a scaled backend pool. One connection carries thousands of requests to one pod; adding pods adds capacity that receives no traffic. This is the section's classic failure and it needs an L7 hop or client-side balancing to fix (Item 114).

  • Not when you need per-request retries. An L4 balancer cannot retry a failed request on another backend because it does not know a request happened. A backend that accepts a connection and then fails every request looks perfectly healthy from L4.

  • Not when the health check must mean anything. A TCP-connect health check confirms a listener is bound, which a process can do while its database pool is exhausted and every request 500s. Deep health requires reading a response — an L7 capability.

  • Not when you want path- or header-based routing, WAF, compression, or readable access logs. All of those require reading the request; an L4 log line has addresses, bytes and duration, and no URL.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "L4 is faster, so it's the better default."

✅ Reality: The latency difference inside a datacentre is a fraction of a millisecond against backends that take tens of milliseconds. What you give up — per-request balancing, retries, routing, deep health checks — routinely costs more availability than the microseconds buy.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "An NLB spreads my gRPC traffic across pods."

✅ Reality: It spreads connections. A gRPC client opens one long-lived HTTP/2 connection and multiplexes everything over it, so a five-client, twenty-pod deployment leaves most pods idle. The load graph looks broken; the balancer is working exactly as specified.

📚 Reference Links

  • The reference L7 balancer — AWS: Application Load Balancers

  • Routing and target-group behaviour — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

  • The full L7 request path, stage by stage — Envoy: Life of a Request

  • Bonus — nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Per what does an L7 balancer balance? Per request — every request on a connection can go to a different backend.
What must it do before it can route? Terminate TLS. It cannot read a path it has not decrypted.
Which retry is safe here? Retry on a connection-level failure or an idempotent method; blind retry of a POST is a duplicate.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An L7 load balancer terminates TLS, parses each HTTP request, and picks a backend per request using the path, headers or method. That unlocks content-based routing, per-request balancing across a fleet, retries on another backend when one fails, deep health checks that read a real response, and access logs with URLs in them. On AWS that is an ALB. The costs are that the balancer now holds your certificate and sees your plaintext, and that it adds a parse-and-re-emit hop — a fraction of a millisecond, which is almost never the thing that matters.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What does "per-request balancing" actually change?

It decouples the client's connection from the backend's. An L7 balancer maintains its own pooled connections to backends; when a request arrives on a client connection it chooses a target at that moment and writes the request onto whichever upstream connection is available. Ten requests on one client connection can land on ten different pods, which is why an L7 hop fixes the HTTP/2 pinning problem that L4 creates.

It also changes what the balancer knows. Because it observes request start and request end, it can implement least-request and EWMA algorithms (Item 109) that L4 cannot — L4 knows how many connections a backend holds, not how much work it is currently doing. And because it sees responses, it can act on them: retry a 502, eject a backend after consecutive 5xx (outlier detection, Item 113), or serve a cached response without contacting anyone.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

ALB or NLB in front of a Kubernetes service mesh?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard cloud-architecture follow-up once a mesh is on the diagram.

🎯 Really testing: whether you notice that a mesh already provides the L7 features, making a second L7 tier partly redundant.

If a mesh sidecar is already doing per-request balancing, retries and mTLS inside the cluster, a second full L7 tier at the edge duplicates that work and adds a second place to configure timeouts and a second TLS termination. The common answer is an NLB in front of the mesh's ingress gateway: L4 gets the packets in cheaply and preserves the source IP, and the gateway — which is Envoy — does the L7 work once.

The counter-argument is that an ALB gives you managed WAF integration, native OIDC authentication and path routing without owning any of it, which is real operational value for teams without a platform group. My tipping point is whether the ingress gateway is already a first-class, well-operated component. If it is, NLB plus gateway is less machinery for the same behaviour; if it is not, the managed L7 tier is worth the duplication.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Capability L7 balancer (ALB, Envoy, nginx) Why it is unavailable at L4
Path / header routing Yes The path is inside the encrypted payload
Per-request balancing Yes L4 pins a connection at SYN time
Retry on another backend Yes, for safe or idempotent requests L4 has no concept of a request boundary
Deep health checks Yes — reads status and body L4 can only confirm a TCP listener
Least-request / EWMA Yes — knows in-flight request count L4 only knows connection count
End-to-end encryption No — it terminates TLS This is the one thing L4 keeps

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Each request is an independent decision, so the balancer's view of backend load is refreshed continuously rather than fixed at connection setup. The practical consequence is smoother distribution: with r requests spread over n backends, skew shrinks as 1/√r rather than being frozen by the connection count, which is why an L7 tier keeps a twenty-pod deployment evenly loaded even with five clients.

The costs are also per-request. Every request pays header parsing, route matching and re-serialisation — tens of microseconds — and the balancer must hold buffers for in-flight requests, which is where its memory scales with concurrency rather than with connection count alone.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not when the payload must be unreadable by your infrastructure. L7 requires termination; if the requirement is genuine end-to-end encryption to the backend, no amount of configuration gets you there.

  • Not for non-HTTP protocols. Terminating a database or broker protocol at an HTTP-aware tier gains nothing and adds a hop that can misparse; use L4.

  • Not when connection volume vastly exceeds request volume — huge numbers of mostly-idle connections, each carrying a handful of requests. You pay L7's per-connection state for balancing decisions you rarely make.

  • Not as an unexamined default for streaming routes. An L7 tier can buffer, compress and time out responses; each of those defaults is wrong for SSE and will silently break token streaming (Item 121).

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "An L7 balancer can retry anything that fails."

✅ Reality: It can retry safely only when the request is idempotent or the failure happened before the backend processed it. Retrying a non-idempotent POST because the response timed out is how you create duplicate orders — the balancer cannot know whether the backend already acted.

❌ Misconception: "L7 adds meaningful latency."

✅ Reality: The parse-and-forward cost is tens of microseconds, and a warm upstream pool typically removes a handshake worth far more than that. The real costs of L7 are the certificate it must hold and the buffering defaults it brings, not the clock.
