📋 Table topic. Per the TABLE / PLAYBOOK rule, Section 4 is the centrepiece and sits above Section 3, Section 6 is discharged by a decision flowchart, Section 5 is omitted, and Section 9 is a set of worked decision walkthroughs.

📚 Reference Links

  • The L4 side, as a product — AWS: Network Load Balancers

  • The L7 side, as a product — AWS: Application Load Balancers

  • What an L7 hop actually does per request — Envoy: Life of a Request

  • L4 proxying in a general-purpose proxy — nginx: ngx_stream_proxy_module

  • Bonus — cloudflare.com/learning: What is a reverse proxy?

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The one-sentence difference? L4 balances connections on the 5-tuple; L7 balances requests on decrypted HTTP.
What does L7 cost you that L4 keeps? End-to-end encryption — L7 must terminate TLS to read anything.
What does L4 cost you that L7 keeps? Per-request balancing, retries, path routing, deep health checks, URLs in logs.
Which one breaks gRPC balancing? L4 — one HTTP/2 connection pins to one backend for its whole life.
Which is cheaper on AWS, and why does that rarely decide it? NLB, by roughly half — but the fleet you under-utilise costs more than the balancer.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The choice is about what the balancer is allowed to see. An L4 balancer decides from the 5-tuple, pins a connection to a backend at the SYN, and never looks inside — protocol-agnostic, near-zero added latency, and the client's TLS stays end-to-end. An L7 balancer terminates TLS and decides per request, which unlocks path routing, retries, least-request algorithms, deep health checks and readable logs. Everything else in the comparison follows from that one line. The trap is choosing L4 for speed on an HTTP/2 service and discovering that one connection pins every request to one pod.

4. Quick Comparison Table — the centrepiece

The full tradeoff table

Dimension L4 (TCP/UDP) L7 (HTTP) When it decides the choice
Decision input 5-tuple: src/dst IP, src/dst port, protocol Method, path, headers, host, cookies You need routing by path or header → L7, no alternative
Balancing unit Per connection, fixed at SYN Per request, re-decided every time Long-lived connections carrying many requests → L7
TLS Untouched; end-to-end to the backend Terminated at the balancer (usually re-encrypted onward) Payload must be unreadable by infra → L4
Visibility in logs Addresses, ports, bytes, duration Full request line, status, upstream, timings Triage matters → L7
Health checks TCP connect / port open HTTP status, path, optionally body "Listener up but app broken" must be caught → L7
Retries Impossible — no request boundary Yes, on connect failures and idempotent requests Backend flakiness must be hidden from clients → L7
Algorithms available Round robin, flow hash, consistent hash + least connections, least request, EWMA, header hash Uneven request cost → L7
Added latency ~microseconds; pass-through can be near zero ~tens to hundreds of microseconds per request Almost never decisive inside a datacentre
Throughput ceiling Very high; scales close to line rate Lower; bounded by parsing and per-request state Millions of pps of non-HTTP traffic → L4
Client source IP Preserved natively (NLB, IPVS) Moved into X-Forwarded-For; socket shows the balancer Backend needs the real IP without header trust → L4
Protocol support Anything over TCP/UDP HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, HTTP/3 where supported Postgres, Kafka, MQTT, game traffic → L4
Static vs dynamic IP NLB gets a static IP / can hold an EIP ALB is DNS-name only, IPs rotate Client can only be configured with an IP → L4
WebSocket / SSE Passes through blindly, no idle-timeout semantics Understood, but subject to buffering and idle timeouts Long-lived streams → L7 with buffering off, or L4
WAF / auth integration None Native (ALB + WAF, OIDC) Managed edge security wanted → L7
AWS cost shape Lower hourly + NLCU, roughly half an ALB Higher hourly + LCU per request/connection/bandwidth Rarely decisive; fleet utilisation dominates
Failure signature Client sees TCP resets; balancer emits nothing Balancer emits 502 / 503 / 504 naming the cause Debuggability → L7

The decision flowchart

The one-line defences, memorised

  • "L7, because I need per-request balancing" — the answer whenever clients hold long-lived connections.

  • "L4, because the backend must hold the only key" — the answer whenever end-to-end encryption is a requirement rather than a preference.

  • "L4 for the packets, L7 for the requests" — the answer for large platforms, which run both: NLB at the edge for a static IP and source-IP preservation, Envoy behind it for everything HTTP.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why can't an L4 balancer route by URL path?

Because the path is inside the TLS record, and an L4 balancer never decrypts. The only application-layer information available before decryption is the SNI in the ClientHello — a hostname, sent in the clear so the server knows which certificate to present. SNI-based routing is therefore possible at L4 and is how TLS pass-through proxies choose a backend pool, but it is hostname granularity and nothing finer.

Even for plaintext HTTP the answer is architectural rather than technical. A balancer that parses HTTP has, by definition, moved to L7: it must buffer until headers are complete, handle request framing, and deal with pipelining and HTTP/2 streams. There is no cheap middle ground where you read the path and keep L4's cost model — reading the path is the cost model.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Same HTTP service, same traffic. At what point does L4 become the wrong answer?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up after someone says "NLB is cheaper and faster".

🎯 Really testing: whether you evaluate by traffic shape rather than by volume.

The flip is driven by the ratio of requests to connections, not by request rate. When clients are browsers, that ratio is small — a handful of requests per connection, thousands of connections — and L4's per-connection hashing spreads load acceptably. When clients are services using HTTP/2, gRPC or an aggressive connection pool, the ratio explodes: one connection carries thousands of requests, and the balancer makes one decision for all of them.

The second flip is heterogeneous request cost. If one endpoint is 2ms and another is 2 seconds, connection-count balancing is measuring the wrong thing entirely; a backend with two connections both running slow queries is far more loaded than one with ten idle ones. Least-request and EWMA fix this, and both require seeing request boundaries.

So the tipping point I would state is: more than a few tens of requests per connection, or more than an order of magnitude spread in request cost, and L4 stops distributing load and starts distributing sockets. Below that, and with no need for routing or retries, L4 is a legitimate simplification.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You migrate an internal API from ALB to NLB to save cost. What breaks first, and how does it present?

📍 Seen in the wild: a real and recurring cost-optimisation regret.

Health-check depth goes first, and it presents as an outage that no dashboard predicted. The ALB was checking GET /healthz and got a 200 that proved the database pool was reachable; the NLB checks that port 8080 accepts a TCP connection, which the process does even when every request fails. A backend with an exhausted connection pool now stays in service indefinitely, taking its share of traffic and 500-ing all of it. Error rate rises to exactly 1/n of traffic and stays there — the flat, partial error rate that is the fingerprint of a shallow health check.

Retries go second, and they present as a step change in client-visible errors. The ALB was quietly retrying connection failures and single 502s onto other targets; nothing at L4 can do that, so failures that used to be invisible now reach clients. Third is source-IP handling in reverse — the backends were reading X-Forwarded-For, and with an NLB there is no such header, so any logic keyed on it now sees an empty value or, worse, a spoofable one the client supplied. The signals that name all three are: a flat non-zero 5xx floor, target-group health flapping to zero without a corresponding deploy, and access logs where the client IP field changed shape on the migration date.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the balancing tiers for a platform serving browser traffic, gRPC service traffic, and a Postgres-compatible endpoint.

🎯 Really testing: whether you resist picking one answer for three different traffic shapes.

The dominating constraint is that these three have nothing in common at the balancing layer, so a single tier will be wrong for at least two of them. Browser traffic wants L7 for routing, WAF and caching. gRPC wants L7 specifically to defeat connection pinning. Postgres wire protocol is not HTTP at all and wants L4, where the only sensible decisions are connection-level anyway.

The shape I would draw is an NLB at the very edge holding the static IPs and preserving source IPs, fronting an Envoy tier that does all HTTP and gRPC work — routing, per-request balancing, retries, mTLS to the mesh. The Postgres endpoint gets its own NLB listener straight to a connection-pooler tier, never touching Envoy, because putting a database protocol through an HTTP proxy buys nothing and risks misparsing. Health checks are deep on the HTTP paths and necessarily shallow on the database path, so the database tier compensates with its own outlier ejection at the pooler.

The first thing I would monitor is per-backend request distribution on the gRPC path, as a ratio of max-to-median requests per pod. It is the metric that proves the L7 tier is actually doing its job, and the one that silently regresses the moment someone puts a "simpler" L4 hop in front of the gateway. Second is health-check depth drift: an alert if any target group's check is a bare TCP check on an HTTP service, because that regression is a one-line Terraform change nobody reviews carefully.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

Discharged by the decision flowchart in Section 4 — the mechanisms themselves belong to Items 106 and 107, which this note exists to compare rather than re-explain.

The one piece of math worth holding here is the skew comparison. With n backends and c connections, an L4 balancer's distribution is balls-in-bins over c: at c = n, roughly 1/e ≈ 37% of backends receive no traffic at all, and skew only becomes acceptable once c ≫ n. An L7 balancer redistributes over r requests instead, and since r ≫ c for any connection-reusing client, its relative skew shrinks as 1/√r. That single inequality — r ≫ c — is the quantitative form of the whole tradeoff.

7. Why It Matters in Production

Getting this wrong does not show up as a latency regression; it shows up as fleet utilisation. An L4 tier in front of connection-reusing clients produces a cluster where a third of the pods are idle and the rest are saturated, so autoscaling adds pods that receive nothing while p99 keeps climbing. The bill goes up, the dashboards look contradictory, and the balancer is behaving exactly as documented.

The observable to name is max-to-median requests per backend. At L7 with least-request it sits near 1.1; at L4 with a handful of long-lived clients it can exceed 3. That ratio is the cheapest possible detector for the most common mistake in this section, and it is not on anyone's default dashboard.

The second observable is 5xx composition. An L7 tier tells you whether a failure was 502, 503 or 504 — unusable response, nowhere healthy to send, or too slow. An L4 tier gives you a TCP reset and leaves the client to guess. Choosing L4 is choosing to debug with less information for the life of the system.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Same backend fleet, two balancers. The difference is what the health check can see.

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "l4" {
  name        = "svc-nlb-tg"
  port        = 8080
  protocol    = "TCP"                 # L4: no notion of a request
  target_type = "ip"
  health_check {
    protocol            = "TCP"       # proves the listener is bound. Nothing more.
    healthy_threshold   = 3
    unhealthy_threshold = 3
  }
}

resource "aws_lb_target_group" "l7" {
  name        = "svc-alb-tg"
  port        = 8080
  protocol    = "HTTP"                # L7: requests are visible
  target_type = "ip"
  health_check {
    protocol = "HTTP"
    path     = "/healthz"             # can assert a real dependency check
    matcher  = "200"                  # a 503 from a degraded pod now ejects it
    interval = 10
    timeout  = 5
  }
}

9. Worked Decision Walkthroughs

Five scenarios run through the Section 4 table, each ending in the choice and the one-sentence defence.

1. A browser-facing REST API behind CloudFront, needing path routing to three services. Checks in order: protocol is HTTP → payload need not stay encrypted to the backend → path routing is required. The requirement for path routing terminates the decision at the first branch that admits only one answer. Choice: L7 (ALB or Envoy). Defence: routing by path is not expressible below L7, so nothing else is a candidate.

2. Internal gRPC between eight caller services and a forty-pod inference gateway. Protocol is gRPC → encryption to backend is desirable but mTLS-after-termination satisfies it → few clients, long-lived HTTP/2 connections. That third check is decisive: eight connections over forty pods leaves most pods idle regardless of algorithm. Choice: L7, and specifically one that speaks HTTP/2 to the backends. Defence: with r ≫ c, only per-request balancing distributes work rather than sockets.

3. A Postgres-compatible endpoint exposed to a partner's VPC. Protocol is not HTTP → the first branch resolves immediately. Adding an HTTP-aware hop would parse nothing useful and risk mangling the wire protocol. Choice: L4. Defence: L7 has no vocabulary for this protocol, so its entire feature set is unavailable by construction.

4. An end-to-end encrypted messaging backend where infrastructure must never hold plaintext. Protocol is HTTP → payload must stay encrypted to the backend. That is the one branch where L4 is mandatory rather than merely acceptable, and it forecloses routing, caching, retries and deep health checks in the same stroke. Choice: L4 pass-through, with SNI routing if multiple pools are needed. Defence: L7 requires the key; if holding the key is disqualifying, the L7 conversation is over.

5. A DNS-over-UDP service handling several million packets per second. Protocol is not HTTP, and the throughput branch would have selected L4 anyway. Per-request state at these rates is the cost, not the benefit. Choice: L4, pass-through, ideally with direct server return. Defence: at this packet rate the balancer must stay a flow-table lookup; anything that allocates per-request state becomes the bottleneck.

10. When TO Use This

  • Reach for L7 as the default for anything HTTP-shaped. Per-request balancing, retries and deep health checks are availability features, and giving them up should be a deliberate decision with a named reason.

  • Reach for L4 when the protocol is not HTTP. Databases, brokers, custom TCP protocols and high-rate UDP have nothing to gain from a parser they will never use.

  • Reach for L4 when the requirement is end-to-end encryption to the backend. This is the one dimension where L7 has no answer at all.

  • Reach for L4 when you need a static IP or genuine source-IP preservation without header trust. An NLB gives both; an ALB gives neither.

  • Run both when the platform is large enough. L4 at the edge for addressing and throughput, L7 behind it for everything request-shaped, is the standard large-platform answer rather than a compromise.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not choose L4 for HTTP/2 or gRPC on latency grounds. The microseconds saved are dwarfed by the fleet you leave idle. This is the single most common expensive mistake in this section.

  • Do not choose L7 when the encryption requirement is real. Terminating "temporarily, we'll fix it later" is how a compliance boundary quietly moves; there is no partial credit here.

  • Do not assume L7 fixes distribution on its own. L7 with plain round robin over heterogeneous request costs is only marginally better than L4; the win comes from least-request or EWMA (Item 109) on top of per-request balancing.

  • Do not stack an L7 tier behind another L7 tier without deciding which one owns retries and timeouts. Two retrying hops multiply load on a struggling backend — three retries at each of two tiers is nine attempts, which is how a slow backend becomes a dead one.

  • Scale limit worth naming: L4 scales close to line rate but cannot balance requests; L7 balances requests but is bounded by per-request state and parsing. Neither limitation is fixable by choosing bigger instances.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "L4 versus L7 is a performance decision."

✅ Reality: It is a visibility decision that has performance consequences. The question is what the balancer is allowed to see; latency differences inside a datacentre are usually two orders of magnitude below backend think-time.

❌ Misconception: "An NLB can't do TLS, so L4 means unencrypted."

✅ Reality: L4 means the balancer does not decrypt — the client's TLS session runs end-to-end to the backend, which is more encryption, not less. (NLB can also terminate TLS if you ask it to, at which point you have given up the property you chose L4 for.)

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Round robin at L4 spreads load evenly."

✅ Reality: It spreads connections evenly, which is only the same thing when every connection carries similar work. With connection reuse, one round-robin decision governs thousands of requests, and the resulting load distribution can be wildly uneven while the connection distribution is perfect.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Answering "L7 is smarter, L4 is faster" and stopping. It is the memorised answer and it survives exactly one follow-up. The version that holds is "L4 decides once per connection from the 5-tuple, L7 decides every request from decrypted HTTP" — a mechanism, from which every row of the table can be re-derived on the spot.

Giving confident latency numbers with no source. "L7 adds a few milliseconds" is both wrong and unsourced; the real figure is tens to hundreds of microseconds per request in-datacentre. Saying "I'd measure it, and I'd expect it well under a millisecond, which is why latency rarely decides this" is a stronger answer than any number you half-remember.

Ignoring the middle of the path. Most real topologies have three or four hops, and the question "which hop terminates TLS" usually has a more interesting answer than "L4 or L7". Answering as if there is exactly one balancer misses where the actual decisions live.

Forgetting health-check depth. It is the most consequential row in the table and the one people omit. A shallow TCP check keeps a broken backend in rotation, and the resulting flat 1/n error rate is a signature worth being able to name.

Stopping at the happy path. No account of what each option does when a backend fails mid-request: L7 can retry an idempotent request elsewhere and emit a precise 502/503/504; L4 can only reset the connection. If failure behaviour never comes up in your answer, you have compared feature lists rather than systems.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
ALB default idle timeout 60 s Kills idle long-lived streams unless raised AWS: Edit load balancer attributes
NLB TCP idle timeout 350 s default, configurable 60–6000 s Raising it above 350 s requires matching the target ENI's TcpEstablishedTimeout AWS: Network Load Balancers
NLB health check protocol options TCP, HTTP, HTTPS TCP is the default shape people accept without thinking AWS: NLB target group health checks
ALB health check default interval 30 s, 5 s timeout Detection lag on an unhealthy target AWS: ALB target group health checks
Idle backends at c = n connections ~37% (1/e) The balls-in-bins result behind L4 skew Balls-in-bins; standard result
L7 per-request parse cost Tens of microseconds Two orders of magnitude below typical backend think-time Envoy: Life of a Request (architecture)

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency L4 adds near zero; L7 adds tens of microseconds per request and usually removes a handshake — the net is often in L7's favour
💰 Cost NLB is roughly half an ALB per hour, and the idle fleet caused by connection pinning costs far more than the difference
🔒 Security / visibility L4 keeps TLS end-to-end and gives you almost no logs; L7 gives you WAF, auth and full access logs and makes the balancer a key holder
📈 Scale L4 scales to line rate but cannot improve distribution; L7 improves distribution but carries per-request state
🔧 Ops complexity L7 brings a timeout hierarchy, buffering defaults and retry policy to tune; L4 brings almost no knobs and almost no control
🐛 Debuggability L7 names the failure (502 / 503 / 504) and logs the URL; L4 gives you a reset and a byte count, permanently

16. Real World Usage

The two-tier edge is the industry default at scale. Large platforms run L4 at the very front — for a static anycast or elastic IP, source-IP preservation and raw packet throughput — and an L7 tier immediately behind it for routing, retries and observability. Google's Maglev and AWS's NLB-in-front-of-ALB pattern are the same architecture reached independently: use each layer for what only it can do.

Model-serving fleets learned this the expensive way. Inference gateways speak HTTP/2 or gRPC and are called by a small number of long-lived clients, which is precisely the shape that L4 balances worst. The public guidance from the gRPC project — use an L7 proxy or client-side balancing, never a plain L4 hop — exists because the failure is common, silent and expensive in GPU hours.

Kubernetes makes both visible at once. A Service of type LoadBalancer gives you L4 and kube-proxy hashing; an Ingress or Gateway gives you L7. Most clusters run both simultaneously, and a surprising amount of "why is one pod hot" debugging is really the discovery that traffic took the L4 path.

📚 Reference Links

  • The algorithm catalogue, with behaviour notes — Envoy: Supported load balancers

  • Least-loaded by latency — Envoy: Peak EWMA load balancer

  • The same algorithms in a general-purpose proxy — nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module

  • Where the choice is exposed on a cloud balancer — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

  • Bonus — Envoy: Life of a Request

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does round robin assume? That every backend and every request cost the same. Both are usually false.
Least connections vs least request — the difference? Connections is an L4 proxy for load; request counts in-flight requests, which HTTP/2 decouples.
What does EWMA add over least request? Latency. It weights by observed response time, so a slow-but-idle backend stops attracting traffic.
What is "power of two choices"? Sample 2 backends at random, pick the less loaded. Near-optimal without global state.
When is consistent hashing the right answer? When the destination must be stable — cache affinity, session affinity, sharded state.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

The algorithm answers one question: given a request and a set of healthy backends, which one gets it? Round robin assumes uniform cost and is fine for uniform workloads. Least connections and least request send work to whoever is holding the least, which handles uneven request cost. EWMA goes further and weights by observed latency, so a degraded backend sheds traffic automatically. Consistent hashing gives up balance deliberately to buy stability — the same key reaches the same backend across scale events. The interesting part is that the first three are trying to equalise load and the last one is trying not to.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is least connections not the same as least loaded?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that a connection is a proxy metric, and a leaky one.

A connection count measures how many sockets a backend holds, which correlates with load only when one connection means one in-flight request. That holds for HTTP/1.1 without pipelining and breaks everywhere else. Under HTTP/2 a single connection can carry a hundred concurrent streams, so a backend with one connection may be doing a hundred times the work of a backend with ten idle ones — and least connections will keep feeding the busy one.

Least request fixes exactly this by counting in-flight requests instead of sockets, which is why it is the sensible default on any L7 proxy and why it is unavailable at L4. Even then it measures concurrency rather than cost: two in-flight requests, one a 2ms lookup and one a 30-second model call, count the same. That residual error is what EWMA addresses by folding in observed latency, so the metric becomes something closer to "expected time until this backend is free".

The hierarchy: connections proxies requests, requests proxies work, and latency is the closest observable to work available without the backend telling you. Each step up costs more state and more sensitivity to noise.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Round robin or least request for an inference fleet where request cost varies 100×?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard model-serving framing; also arrives as "why is one GPU at 100% and the rest idle?"

🎯 Really testing: whether you connect cost variance to queueing rather than to averages.

With uniform cost, round robin and least request converge — over enough requests both spread evenly, and round robin is cheaper and has no state. The moment cost variance is large, they diverge sharply, and the reason is queueing rather than fairness. Round robin will hand a backend a new request while it is still generating a 2,000-token response, because it counts turns, not work. Queues form on the unlucky backends, and tail latency climbs while average utilisation looks healthy.

Least request keeps a backend out of rotation while it is busy, so the queue forms at the balancer where it is visible and drainable rather than inside one worker where it is not. For inference specifically, this is worth more than it sounds: a request stuck behind a long generation on a saturated GPU can wait seconds, and no amount of horizontal scaling fixes a distribution problem.

The tipping point is the spread in request cost. Below roughly 2×, round robin is fine and simpler; above it — inference, search and report generation are all well above — least request is the floor. One caveat: least request needs honest in-flight accounting, and a proxy that stops counting a streaming response at first byte is back to round robin with extra steps.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You add ten pods to a fifty-pod fleet under least request. What happens in the first thirty seconds?

📍 Seen in the wild: the "thundering herd on scale-out" question; also asked as "why did our new pods fall over immediately?"

The new pods have zero in-flight requests, so least request sends them everything. Ten empty backends against fifty warm ones is an absorbing state for a naive least-request implementation: every arriving request goes to whichever pod has the lowest count, and the new pods have the lowest count until they are as loaded as everyone else. They receive a burst far above their steady-state share, hit cold caches, cold JIT, unwarmed connection pools and — for model servers — unloaded weights, and their latency is terrible precisely when they are receiving the most traffic.

It presents as a latency spike correlated with deploys rather than traffic, and new-pod error rates far above fleet average for the first minute. Shallow health checks leave the pods in rotation while failing; strict ones flap them out, which is worse, because the herd simply moves to the next new pod. Mitigations: slow start (ramp a new backend's weight from zero over a warm-up window — nginx, Envoy and ALB all support it), power of two choices instead of global least request, so empty-pod attraction is probabilistic rather than absolute, and readiness probes that only pass once warm-up is genuinely done. Slow start is the one people forget, and it is one directive.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the balancing strategy for a platform with a stateless API, a session-affine WebSocket tier, and a sharded cache.

🎯 Really testing: whether you can hold three different objectives at once — equalise, stabilise, and shard — instead of picking one algorithm for the platform.

The highest-stakes constraint is that these three want different things. The stateless API wants load equalisation: any backend can serve any request, so the objective is minimising queueing, and least request with power-of-two-choices plus slow start is the answer. The WebSocket tier wants stability for the life of a connection but has no cross-connection state, so plain least-connections at connect time is enough — affinity is implicit in the connection, and no hashing is needed.

The sharded cache wants stability of key-to-node mapping, which is a different objective entirely: it is willing to accept imbalance to avoid remapping. That is consistent hashing with bounded loads — plain consistent hashing gives stability but tolerates hot shards, and the bounded-load variant caps how overloaded any node may get before keys spill to the next node in the ring. The composition rule worth saying out loud is that hashing should be applied to the smallest hop that needs it: hash at the cache tier, not at the edge, or you have made your whole front door affinity-bound to serve one component's requirement.

The failure mode I would monitor first is max-to-median requests per backend on the API tier, alerting above about 1.5, because it detects both a wrong algorithm and a broken slow start. For the cache tier the metric is key-space movement per scale event — with consistent hashing it should be roughly 1/n of keys and anything larger means the ring is misconfigured or virtual nodes are too few. A single hot shard at 3× the median is the third alert, and it is the one that says the key distribution, not the algorithm, is the problem.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Algorithm What it measures Available at Cost of state When you'd actually pick it
Round robin Turn order L4 and L7 None Uniform request cost, uniform backends, and you want the simplest thing that works
Weighted round robin Turn order × static weight L4 and L7 None Heterogeneous instance sizes, or a canary receiving 5%
Least connections Open sockets per backend L4 and L7 Per-backend counter HTTP/1.1 or raw TCP where one connection ≈ one unit of work
Least request (least outstanding) In-flight requests L7 only Per-backend counter The sane L7 default; handles uneven request cost
Power of two choices (P2C) Sample 2, take the lighter L7 (usually with least request) None global Large fleets, or wherever global least-request causes herding
Peak EWMA / least-loaded Recent latency × in-flight L7 only Per-backend moving average Backends degrade gracefully rather than failing; slow nodes must shed traffic
IP hash / hash-by-header Hash of a chosen key L4 (IP) and L7 (any header) None Crude affinity when you cannot change the client
Consistent hashing (ring / maglev) Hash of key onto a ring L4 and L7 Ring, rebuilt on membership change Cache or shard affinity that must survive scale events
Random Nothing L4 and L7 None Baseline; surprisingly close to round robin at high fanout, and immune to synchronisation

5. Memory Hook (Story Form)

Design axis: how much does the balancer know about what each backend is currently doing?

📖 Story — the supermarket checkout

  • Round robin — you send each shopper to the next till in order, without looking at the queues.

  • Weighted round robin — two of the tills are double-width, so they get two shoppers per rotation.

  • Least connections — you send each shopper to the till with the fewest people standing at it, whatever is in their trolleys.

  • Least request — you count items being scanned right now rather than people standing there, so a till with one full trolley outranks a till with three empty-handed shoppers.

  • Power of two choices — you glance at two tills picked at random and send the shopper to the shorter one, because looking at all thirty takes longer than the saving.

  • Peak EWMA — you remember which cashiers have been slow all morning and route around them even when their queue looks short.

  • Consistent hashing — shoppers whose surname starts with A–F always go to till 3, so till 3 already knows their loyalty card; when a till closes, only its letters move.

🗺️ Story → Mechanism Mapping

  • Queue length = connection count · items being scanned = in-flight requests · cashier speed = observed latency

  • Glancing at two tills = P2C's O(1) sampling that avoids the herding of global minimum selection

  • Surname buckets = hash keys; a till closing moving only its letters = the 1/n reshuffle property of consistent hashing

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The algorithms differ in the metric they minimise; the math is where the differences become concrete.

Round robin is a counter modulo n. Zero state, perfectly fair in turns, and blind to cost. Its weakness is quantified by queueing theory: when service times vary, mean queue length grows with the variance of service time, so round robin's latency penalty scales with cost variance even at identical throughput.

Least request selects argmin(in_flight[i]). It approximates join-shortest-queue, which is optimal for identical servers — but a global minimum has a herding problem: every balancer instance sees the same minimum and sends to the same backend simultaneously.

Power of two choices is the fix, and the math is the reason it is everywhere. Sampling two backends at random and taking the lighter reduces maximum load from Θ(log n / log log n) — the balls-in-bins result for pure random assignment — to Θ(log log n). That is an exponential improvement for two samples, and going to three or more buys almost nothing on top. It is the best cost-to-benefit ratio in this list: O(1) work, no global state, near-optimal balance.

Peak EWMA maintains an exponentially weighted moving average of response latency per backend and scores each as roughly cost = ewma_latency × (in_flight + 1), picking the minimum. The exponential weighting means recent observations dominate, so a backend that starts degrading sheds traffic within seconds rather than after its average drags down. The tuning risk is the decay constant: too fast and it oscillates on noise, too slow and it is least-request with extra machinery.

Consistent hashing places both backends and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next backend clockwise. Adding or removing one of n backends remaps an expected 1/n of keys rather than nearly all of them, which is the entire reason it exists. Virtual nodes (typically 100–200 replicas per backend) smooth the otherwise lumpy arc distribution.

The sequence above is the whole argument for EWMA in one exchange: least request and EWMA disagree exactly when a backend is idle because it is slow, which is what a degrading node looks like from outside.

7. Why It Matters in Production

The algorithm is the difference between a fleet you can size from average load and one you cannot. Under a well-chosen algorithm, adding capacity reduces p99; under a poorly chosen one, adding capacity leaves p99 flat while the bill rises, because the new capacity is not receiving proportional work.

The observable is max-to-median requests (or in-flight requests) per backend. Under least request with P2C it sits close to 1.1–1.2. Under round robin with high cost variance it drifts to 2× or more. Under L4 balancing of HTTP/2 traffic it can exceed 5×. That one ratio detects the entire family of failures in this note and belongs on the same dashboard as p99.

The second observable is p99 immediately after a scale-out: a correctly configured fleet improves within the warm-up window, while one without slow start gets worse for thirty seconds after every deploy — routinely misattributed to the deploy process rather than to the balancer.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# nginx: the three most common choices, one upstream block each
upstream api_uniform {
  server 10.0.1.11:8080;
  server 10.0.1.12:8080;              # default is round robin - no directive needed
}

upstream api_variable_cost {
  least_conn;                          # nginx OSS counts connections, not requests
  server 10.0.1.11:8080 slow_start=30s;   # ramp weight over 30s to avoid the new-pod herd
  server 10.0.1.12:8080 slow_start=30s;   # (slow_start requires NGINX Plus)
}

upstream cache_tier {
  hash $request_uri consistent;        # consistent hashing: same URI to the same cache node
  server 10.0.2.21:11211;
  server 10.0.2.22:11211;
  server 10.0.2.23:11211;
}

# Envoy: the L7-only options nginx OSS does not expose
lb_policy: LEAST_REQUEST          # counts in-flight requests, not sockets
least_request_lb_config:
  choice_count: 2                 # power of two choices - the default, and the right one
slow_start_config:
  slow_start_window: 30s          # linear ramp for newly healthy hosts

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Three pods behind the Envoy config above. A 2-second generation request is already running on pod A when three short requests arrive.

🎬 t=0.0s   state: A in-flight 1 (long, ~2000ms) | B in-flight 0 | C in-flight 0
    │
    ▼
📥 [1] req-1 arrives → P2C samples {A, C} → C has 0, A has 1 → C  .......... C: 1
    │
    ▼
📥 [2] req-2 arrives → P2C samples {A, B} → B has 0, A has 1 → B  .......... B: 1
    │
    ▼
📥 [3] req-3 arrives → P2C samples {B, C} → tie at 1 → random → B  ......... B: 2
    │   ⚠️ round robin would have sent one of these to A, queueing it behind 2000ms
    ▼
⏱️ t=0.05s  req-1 and req-2 complete (~45ms each)  ......................... B: 1, C: 0
    │
    ▼
🎬 [4] new pod D becomes healthy, in-flight 0, slow_start_window 30s
    │   global least-request would send D everything; weight ramps 0→100% linearly
    ▼
📥 [5] req-4 → P2C samples {A, D} → D chosen, but weighted at ~10% at t=3s
    │
    ▼
✅ [6] steady state at t=30s: max/median in-flight ≈ 1.1 across A–D

  1. The long request on A is why least request beats round robin here. Round robin's next turn was A's, and req-1 would have queued behind a 2-second generation for no reason other than turn order. Least request removed A from consideration for the whole duration of that request, automatically.

  2. P2C sampled rather than scanned. With four backends the difference is negligible; with four hundred, a global minimum scan is both expensive and herding — every balancer replica would converge on the same "least loaded" pod at the same instant. Sampling two makes the choice good and the herd statistical.

  3. The tie at step 3 was broken randomly, not deterministically. Deterministic tie-breaking is a subtle source of skew: with many balancer instances and frequent ties, a fixed rule (lowest index, first in list) sends every tie to the same backend.

  4. Slow start is what makes step 4 safe. Without it, pod D's in-flight count of zero makes it the minimum of every sample it appears in, and it receives a burst several times its steady-state share while its caches are cold. The linear weight ramp converts that burst into a gradient.

  5. The steady-state number is the one to quote. Max-to-median in-flight of ~1.1 is what a healthy least-request-plus-P2C fleet looks like. If yours is 2 or 3, the algorithm is not the problem you think it is — check for connection pinning (Item 114) before changing algorithms.

10. When TO Use This

  • Least request with power-of-two-choices, plus slow start: the default for any L7 HTTP fleet. It handles cost variance, avoids herding, and survives scale events. Choosing anything else should have a stated reason.

  • Round robin when request cost is genuinely uniform and you value simplicity. Static asset serving, health-check endpoints, and stateless transforms with fixed cost do not need anything cleverer.

  • Peak EWMA when backends degrade rather than fail. GPU nodes with thermal throttling, databases with a slow replica, and any fleet where "slow" is more common than "down" benefit from latency-aware selection.

  • Consistent hashing when a stable destination is the requirement. Cache tiers, sharded stateful services, and rate limiters that must count in one place — anywhere remapping is more expensive than imbalance.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not use least connections at L4 for HTTP/2 traffic. Connections are decoupled from work under multiplexing, so the metric is measuring something that no longer correlates with load; you will confidently balance the wrong thing (Item 114).

  • Do not use global least request across many balancer replicas without P2C. Every replica computes the same minimum and stampedes the same backend; the fix is sampling, and it is usually a one-line config change.

  • Do not use consistent hashing for stateless services "because it sounds better". You are trading away load equalisation for a stability property you do not need, and you inherit hot-key risk: one popular key means one hot backend, permanently.

  • Do not deploy least request without slow start on a fleet that scales. Empty backends are maximally attractive to least request, so every scale-out and every deploy sends a burst at your coldest instances.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Round robin is fair."

✅ Reality: It is fair in turns, not in work. Two backends receiving equal request counts can be carrying wildly different loads if the requests differ in cost — and cost variance is the normal case, not the exception, for anything that queries, renders or generates.

❌ Misconception: "Consistent hashing is a load balancing algorithm like the others."

✅ Reality: It optimises a different objective. The others minimise imbalance; consistent hashing minimises remapping and accepts imbalance as the price. Comparing them on evenness misses that they are answering different questions.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Sampling two backends must be worse than checking all of them."

✅ Reality: Sampling two takes maximum load from Θ(log n / log log n) to Θ(log log n) — an exponential improvement — and it avoids the herding that a global minimum creates across multiple balancer replicas. Checking all of them is both more expensive and, in a distributed balancer tier, actively worse.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Naming an algorithm without naming the metric it minimises. "We use least connections" is a config fact; "we use least connections because at L4 that is the closest available proxy for in-flight work, and it stops being one under HTTP/2" is an answer. The metric is the substance.

Ignoring what happens on membership change. Every algorithm has scale-out behaviour, and it is where the production failures live: the new-pod herd under least request, the full remap under modulo hashing, the ring rebuild under consistent hashing. If your answer covers only steady state, you have described half the algorithm.

Quoting balance numbers with no source. "It balances well" invites the question you cannot answer; cite the ratio you actually watch — max-to-median in-flight per backend — and the value you expect.

Stopping before the interaction with health checks. An algorithm only selects among backends the health checker says are healthy, so a shallow health check silently poisons every algorithm in this list. The two topics are one system, and answering as if the candidate set is always correct is the most common omission here.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
P2C maximum load Θ(log log n) vs Θ(log n / log log n) for random Two samples; three or more add little Balanced allocations / power-of-two-choices result
Consistent hashing remap on membership change ~1/n of keys Versus ~all keys for modulo hashing Consistent hashing, standard result
Virtual nodes per backend, typical 100–200 Fewer produces visibly lumpy arc distribution Common implementation guidance (Envoy ring hash minimum_ring_size)
Envoy least_request default choice_count 2 P2C is the default, not an opt-in Envoy: Supported load balancers
Typical healthy max/median in-flight per backend ~1.1–1.2 The number to alert above 1.5 on Operational rule of thumb — measure yours
Slow-start window, common setting 30 s Long enough for cache and pool warm-up on most services nginx slow_start, Envoy slow_start_window

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Better algorithms move queueing from inside a backend to the balancer, which improves p99 far more than p50
💰 Cost Poor balancing shows up as capacity you pay for and do not use; the max/median ratio is a direct multiplier on fleet size
🔒 Security / visibility Hash-based affinity leaks a little structure — an attacker who controls the hash key can target a specific backend
📈 Scale Global-minimum algorithms herd as balancer replicas multiply; P2C is what keeps selection O(1) and uncoordinated
🔧 Ops complexity EWMA and slow start add tuning parameters that need a reason and a review; round robin has none to get wrong
🐛 Debuggability Latency-aware algorithms make load distribution time-varying, so "why did this request go there" stops having a static answer

16. Real World Usage

Envoy defaults to power-of-two-choices for least request, which is the clearest signal available that the theory is settled in practice: the reference L7 proxy ships the sampling variant rather than the global minimum, because the herding problem is real at fleet scale.

Consistent hashing entered mainstream infrastructure through caching. The original motivation — a memcached tier where adding a node must not invalidate the whole cache — is still the clearest use case, and the same ring reappears in database sharding and in sticky routing for stateful sessions.

Model-serving stacks have made least-request the de facto standard. Generation cost varies by orders of magnitude, so turn-order balancing produces exactly the queueing pathology theory predicts. Serving frameworks converge on in-flight-aware routing, sometimes extended with backend-reported queue depth — that variant belongs to the LLM serving folder, not here.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • EWMA — Exponentially Weighted Moving Average: each new latency observation is blended into a running average with an exponential decay, so recent samples dominate and a degrading backend is detected in seconds rather than after its lifetime average shifts.

  • P2C — Power of Two Choices: sample two candidates at random, pick the lighter. The name is the mechanism.

  • 110-consistent-hashing.md — the one entry in the table with a different objective, in depth

  • 111-sticky-sessions.md — affinity as a requirement rather than a strategy

  • 112-health-checks.md — the candidate set every algorithm here selects from

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Client-side load balancing — the algorithm runs in the caller, using a resolver rather than a proxy (Item 114)

  • Queue-based work distribution — workers pull instead of being pushed to, which makes the balancing problem disappear (Section 10)

  • Backend-reported load signals — the backend advertises its own utilisation rather than the balancer inferring it

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Slow start — the ramp that makes least request safe across deploys (Item 113)

  • Outlier detection — removes backends the algorithm should never have been offered (Item 113)

  • Autoscaling — changes membership, which is exactly when algorithm choice matters most

📚 Reference Links

  • Ring hash and Maglev, as shipped — Envoy: Supported load balancers

  • The same thing in nginx — nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module — hash ... consistent

  • Where it appears at the balancer — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What problem does it solve? Membership changes remap ~1/n of keys instead of ~all of them.
What does modulo hashing do on scale-out? hash % n → hash % (n+1) remaps almost every key. Cache tier goes cold at once.
Why virtual nodes? A few points on the ring distribute arcs unevenly; 100–200 replicas per node smooth it.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Consistent hashing exists because hash % n is catastrophic when n changes: add one node to a ten-node cache and roughly 90% of keys move, so the tier goes cold in an instant. Consistent hashing puts nodes and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only the keys in that node's arc — an expected 1/n of the key space. The price is that arcs are uneven unless you add virtual nodes, and that a single hot key still lands on a single node.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through what happens on the ring when a node dies.

Both keys and nodes are hashed into the same space — conventionally a 32- or 64-bit ring. A key is owned by the first node encountered walking clockwise from the key's position. When a node disappears, only the keys that sat in the arc between it and its predecessor need a new owner, and they all move to the next node clockwise. Every other key's lookup is unchanged, because no other node's successor relationship moved.

Virtual nodes are what make that arc small and uniform. With one point per physical node, arcs are drawn from a random distribution and vary widely — a node can own three times its share by luck alone, and its failure dumps that whole arc onto one successor. With 100–200 virtual points per node, each physical node owns many small scattered arcs, so its share converges on 1/n and its failure spreads across many successors rather than one. Envoy exposes this as ring size, nginx as hash ... consistent.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Consistent hashing or least request in front of a cache tier?

🎯 Really testing: whether you recognise that these optimise different objectives and cannot be compared on evenness.

Least request equalises load and destroys locality: the same key goes to a different cache node each time, so every node ends up caching every key. Hit ratio collapses toward what a single node's memory can hold divided across the fleet, and you have bought fair CPU distribution with a much smaller effective cache.

Consistent hashing preserves locality and accepts imbalance. Each key lives on one node, so the fleet's effective cache is the sum of its memory rather than a replicated fraction, and hit ratio scales with the fleet. The costs are hot keys — one viral object saturates one node permanently — and a rebalance on every membership change, small though it is.

The tipping point is whether the backend holds state derived from the key. If it does — a cache, a shard, a session, a rate-limit counter — hashing wins and the imbalance is the cost of doing business. If it does not, hashing is giving up equalisation for nothing. The middle ground worth naming is consistent hashing with bounded loads, which caps how overloaded any node may become before spilling keys to the next node on the ring; it keeps most of the locality and removes the worst of the hot-key risk.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Modulo hashing Consistent hashing (ring) Consistent hashing, bounded loads Maglev hashing
Remap on ±1 node ~all keys ~1/n of keys ~1/n plus spill Slightly more than 1/n
Even distribution Good Needs virtual nodes Enforced by a load cap Very even by construction
Hot-key protection None None Yes — spills past a cap None
Lookup cost O(1) O(log n) ring search O(log n) plus check O(1) table lookup
When you'd actually pick it Fixed node count that never changes The general default for cache and shard affinity Skewed key popularity Very large fleets needing O(1) and minimal disruption

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The math is the reason to use it. With n nodes, removing one moves the keys in that node's arcs — an expected fraction 1/n of the key space — while modulo hashing moves an expected 1 − 1/n. At n = 10 that is 10% versus 90%; at n = 100, 1% versus 99%. The gap widens as the fleet grows, which is exactly backwards from what you want under modulo.

Virtual nodes control variance rather than the mean. With v virtual points per node, the standard deviation of each node's share of the ring falls roughly as 1/√v, so v = 1 gives wildly uneven arcs and v = 100–200 brings each node within a few percent of 1/n. The cost is memory for the ring and O(log(n·v)) lookup, both trivial at realistic sizes. Maglev trades the ring for a fixed-size lookup table, buying O(1) lookup and very even distribution at the cost of slightly more disruption on membership change.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not for stateless backends. If any backend can serve any request equally well, hashing buys stability you do not need and forfeits load equalisation you do. Least request is strictly better there.

  • Not when key popularity is skewed and you have no bounded-load variant. One hot key means one hot node, permanently, and no amount of scaling helps because the key cannot move. Bounded loads or key splitting is required first.

  • Not as a substitute for session storage. Hashing a session to a node makes that node's failure a user-visible logout; externalising session state removes the requirement entirely, which is the better fix (Item 111).

  • Not with a key you do not control the cardinality of. Hashing on a header that takes three values distributes traffic across three nodes regardless of how many you run — a real and embarrassing failure mode.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Consistent hashing distributes load evenly."

✅ Reality: It distributes the key space evenly, given enough virtual nodes. Load is even only if key popularity is uniform, which it almost never is. Evenness is the property it is weakest at, not the one it is for.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The 1/n guarantee means only 1/n of requests are affected when a node dies."

✅ Reality: 1/n of the key space moves. If the dead node held disproportionately popular keys, the traffic impact is much larger than 1/n, and the successor node inherits all of it at once — which is how one failure becomes two.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 112-health-checks.md — health changes are membership changes, so a flapping check thrashes the ring

  • Sharding and replication in the HLD folder — the same ring, applied to data ownership rather than routing

Cookie-based or IP-hash affinity — what actually differs?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Your WebSocket chat tier needs affinity. Sticky sessions, or something else?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Cookie-based stickiness on a managed balancer — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

  • ip_hash and hash-based affinity — nginx: ngx_http_upstream_module

  • Session affinity in a modern L7 proxy — Envoy: Supported load balancers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Two ways to implement it? Balancer-issued cookie (L7), or hash of a stable key such as source IP (L4/L7).
Why is ip_hash a poor affinity key? Corporate NAT collapses thousands of users onto one backend; mobile IPs change mid-session.
Why is it a scaling smell? It converts a stateless tier into a stateful one — deploys, scale-in and failures become user-visible.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Session affinity pins a client to a backend so that state living in that backend's memory stays reachable — a WebSocket, an in-progress upload, a local session cache. The balancer implements it with a cookie it issues and reads, or by hashing something stable like the source IP. It works, and it is almost always a signal that state is in the wrong place: the moment a backend is pinned, scale-in drops sessions, deploys drop sessions, and load stops being redistributable. WebSocket connections are the one case where affinity is inherent rather than chosen, because the connection is the state.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Cookie-based or IP-hash affinity — what actually differs?

A cookie is issued by the balancer, carries an opaque reference to the chosen target, and is returned by the client on every subsequent request. It is precise: exactly one client, exactly one target, with an expiry the balancer controls. It requires L7, because the balancer must read and write headers, and it fails for clients that do not keep cookies — native apps, some SDKs, server-to-server callers.

IP hash needs no client cooperation and works at L4, which is its only advantage. Its accuracy is poor in both directions: a corporate NAT or mobile carrier CGNAT maps thousands of distinct users onto one address, so they all land on one backend and the fleet is skewed by the client's network topology rather than by your traffic. And a single user's address changes when they move between WiFi and cellular, breaking the affinity precisely when they are most likely to notice.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Your WebSocket chat tier needs affinity. Sticky sessions, or something else?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up whenever WebSocket appears on a design.

🎯 Really testing: whether you distinguish affinity that is inherent to a connection from affinity used to paper over in-memory state.

For the connection itself, there is no choice to make: a WebSocket is a single TCP connection to a single backend, so it is affine by construction. No configuration creates that and none removes it; the balancer just has to not interfere, which mostly means idle timeouts long enough to survive quiet periods and a graceful drain on shutdown.

The real question is what happens to the other users in the same conversation. If the design assumes both participants are pinned to the same backend, you have built a system that only works while they happen to hash together, and it will fail as soon as the fleet grows. The answer that scales is a fan-out layer — Redis pub/sub, a message bus, or a purpose-built presence service — so a message published on any backend reaches subscribers on every backend. Affinity then covers only the connection, which is inherent, and no shared state depends on it.

That reframing is the whole point: accept affinity where the protocol imposes it, and design so that nothing else depends on it. The tell that you have got it wrong is a deploy that drops user state rather than merely reconnecting sockets.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Approach Granularity Survives client IP change Survives backend loss When you'd actually pick it
Balancer cookie Per client Yes No — session is gone L7 traffic from browsers where affinity is genuinely required
Application cookie Per client, app-defined Yes No You need affinity to follow an app-level identity, not a balancer's opaque id
IP hash Per source address No No L4 only, and you have no better key
Consistent hash on a header Per chosen key Yes, if the key is stable Only that key's share moves Sharded state where the key is meaningful (Item 110)
No affinity + externalised state None needed n/a Yes — any backend serves The default you should be arguing toward

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The mechanism is a bypass: for every request carrying a valid affinity cookie, the load balancing algorithm is skipped. That is the source of every consequence. Load can no longer be redistributed, so the balance you get is whatever the initial assignment happened to produce; a backend that is unlucky in its first hour stays unlucky. And because the affinity outlives the backend, the failure path in the diagram is the normal path during every deploy.

The cost is quantifiable. With n backends and sticky sessions of average length T, removing one backend orphans 1/n of active sessions immediately, and a rolling deploy that replaces all n backends over a window shorter than T orphans effectively all of them. That is the arithmetic behind "our deploys log everyone out": it is not a bug in the deploy, it is the design.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not to compensate for in-memory session state. Externalise the session to Redis or a signed token and the requirement disappears, along with the deploy problem, the scale-in problem and the skew. This is the fix in the large majority of cases.

  • Not with ip_hash for public traffic. Carrier-grade NAT and corporate egress collapse enormous user populations onto single addresses; you will discover this as one backend at 5× the load of its peers with no explanation in your own traffic.

  • Not on a fleet that autoscales aggressively. Scale-in events destroy sessions by definition, so the more elastic the fleet, the more user-visible damage affinity does.

  • Not for long-lived affinity windows "to be safe". A multi-hour cookie TTL means a backend that came up during a traffic peak keeps its share of load through the trough, and skew persists long after the reason for it has gone.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Sticky sessions improve performance because the cache is warm."

✅ Reality: Sometimes, marginally — and at the cost of making load undistributable, deploys destructive and scale-in user-visible. If per-backend cache warmth is genuinely the goal, that is a hashing decision on a meaningful key (Item 110), not a session-affinity one.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "WebSocket requires sticky sessions to be enabled on the load balancer."

✅ Reality: A WebSocket is one TCP connection to one backend — it is affine whether or not stickiness is configured. What it actually needs from the balancer is an idle timeout longer than the quiet periods and a graceful drain on shutdown. Enabling cookie stickiness for a WebSocket tier is a no-op that people mistake for the fix.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 109-load-balancing-algorithms.md — affinity is a bypass of whichever algorithm you chose

  • 08-realtime-streaming/ WebSocket notes — the one case where affinity is inherent

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 110-consistent-hashing.md — affinity done as deliberate sharding rather than as a workaround

  • 113-outlier-detection-circuit-breaking.md — connection draining, which is what makes losing a sticky backend survivable

  • 114-grpc-http2-load-balancing.md — the other place where a long-lived connection pins traffic you wanted spread
