📚 Reference Links

  • The canonical treatment, including the failure modes — Amazon Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

  • Active health checking in an L7 proxy — Envoy: Health checking

  • Passive ejection, the other half — Envoy: Outlier detection

  • Managed-balancer defaults and thresholds — AWS: Health checks for Application Load Balancer target groups

  • Bonus — kubernetes.io: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Active vs passive? Active = the balancer probes on a timer. Passive = it infers health from real request outcomes.
Shallow vs deep? Shallow: is the process listening? Deep: can it actually serve, dependencies included.
How does a deep health check cause an outage? A shared dependency blips → every backend reports unhealthy → the whole fleet is removed at once.
What is fail-open (fail-static)? When all backends are unhealthy, keep serving to all of them rather than serving to none.
Liveness vs readiness in Kubernetes? Liveness failure restarts the pod. Readiness failure only removes it from Service endpoints.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A health check decides which backends the load balancing algorithm is allowed to choose from — so it is an availability control, not a monitoring feature. Active checks probe on a timer; passive checks watch real request outcomes and eject backends that fail them. The depth is the interesting axis: a TCP-connect check proves a listener is bound while every request 500s, and a deep check that touches a shared database can mark the entire fleet unhealthy the moment that database blips. The rule that saves you is fail-open: when everything looks unhealthy, assume the checker is wrong and keep serving.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What does each check depth actually prove?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can predict which failures a given check will miss.

A TCP-connect check proves that something has bound the port and the kernel completes a handshake. It survives a fully wedged application: an exhausted thread pool, a deadlocked worker, a process that accepts connections and never replies. It is the cheapest check and the easiest to misplace trust in.

An HTTP check on a trivial endpoint — a /ping that returns a static 200 — proves the HTTP stack and the request-handling path are alive. It catches the wedged-worker case that TCP misses. It still passes when every real endpoint fails, because it touches none of the code they use.

A deep check exercises real dependencies: a database ping, a cache read, a check that model weights are loaded. It proves the backend can do its job — and it couples the backend's reported health to the health of everything it depends on, which is where the danger begins. The middle position most services should hold is a local deep check: verify things that are true of this instance — pool initialised, config loaded, disk writable, warm-up complete — and deliberately exclude shared dependencies, because a shared dependency failing is not a reason to remove this instance rather than that one.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How aggressive should the thresholds be?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after any "we had a flapping backend" story.

🎯 Really testing: whether you see detection speed and stability as a single tradeoff with a named cost on each side.

Fast detection means short intervals and low unhealthy thresholds — say a 5-second interval and 2 consecutive failures, so a dead backend leaves rotation in about 10 seconds. The cost is false positives: a GC pause, a brief network hiccup or a slow disk flush now ejects a healthy backend, and if it ejects several at once the survivors take the load and fail the same check. That is how a threshold tuned for speed manufactures the outage it was meant to detect.

Slow detection is the mirror: a 30-second interval with 3 failures leaves a dead backend serving errors for a minute and a half, and at n backends that is 1/n of traffic failing for that whole window. Asymmetric thresholds are the standard resolution — quick to eject, slow to re-admit (AWS's defaults are deliberately shaped this way, with a higher healthy threshold than unhealthy) — because a flapping backend that re-enters rotation early does more damage than one that stays out a little too long.

My default is a 10-second interval, 2 failures to eject, 3 successes to restore, and a check timeout well below the interval so a slow check cannot overlap itself. Then I make it irrelevant by adding passive outlier detection on real traffic, which detects genuine failure in one request rather than in n × interval seconds.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

Your deep health check queries the database. The database has a 30-second blip. Walk me through it.

📍 Seen in the wild: one of the best-documented cascading-failure patterns; the Builders' Library article exists largely because of it.

Every backend fails the check simultaneously, because they all share the dependency. Within one or two intervals the balancer marks the entire target group unhealthy. What happens next depends entirely on whether the balancer fails open. If it does not, it has zero healthy targets and returns 503 to everything — a total outage caused by a database blip that the application layer would have survived with a handful of slow requests and some retries. If it does fail open, it keeps distributing to all targets, most requests succeed on cached paths, and the incident stays a partial degradation.

The recovery is worse than the failure. The database returns, health checks pass, and all n backends re-enter rotation at once carrying no warm state while a queue of retrying clients arrives together — a thundering herd against a database that has just recovered, which frequently knocks it over again. The signals that name this correctly are healthy-host-count dropping to zero with no deploy, 503s with zero backend log entries (the balancer never forwarded anything), and a sawtooth in healthy-host-count as the fleet oscillates. The fixes are structural, not tuning: exclude shared dependencies from health checks, fail open when the unhealthy fraction crosses a threshold (Envoy's panic threshold is 50% by default), and add jitter to check timing so n backends do not probe in lockstep.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the health-checking strategy for a GPU inference fleet where pods take three minutes to load model weights.

🎯 Really testing: whether you separate "is it alive", "is it ready" and "is it performing" into three different signals with three different consequences.

The dominating constraint is the warm-up: a pod that is alive but has no weights loaded must receive no traffic, and must not be killed for taking too long. That is exactly the split Kubernetes encodes. A startup probe with a generous failure budget covers the three-minute load and suppresses the other probes while it runs, so nothing kills the pod for being slow to start. A readiness probe then gates traffic on weights-loaded plus warm-up inference completed — local state only, never a check against a shared model registry or a vector store, or one registry blip empties the fleet. A liveness probe stays deliberately shallow and slow, because restarting a GPU pod costs three minutes of capacity and should require strong evidence, not a single slow response.

Between the balancer and the pods, the interesting hop is the ingress: it should trust readiness for membership but add passive outlier detection on real requests, because a GPU that is thermally throttling or has a corrupted CUDA context will pass an HTTP readiness check while serving garbage or timing out. Passive detection catches degraded-but-responsive, which is the dominant failure mode for accelerators; active checks catch dead, which is the rarer one.

The failure I would monitor first is healthy-host-count against fleet size, alerting on any drop below the panic threshold rather than on individual ejections, because the correlated case is the dangerous one. Second is time-from-pod-start-to-first-successful-request, which is the number that tells you whether your startup probe budget is honest — if it drifts up toward the probe's limit, the next model version will start failing to launch, and it will look like a deploy problem rather than a probe problem.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Active health check Passive health check / outlier detection
Trigger Timer, independent of traffic Real request outcomes
Detection latency interval × threshold — seconds to a minute One to a few requests
Cost n_backends × n_balancers probes, always Free — reuses traffic you already have
Works with no traffic Yes No — nothing to observe
Catches "listening but broken" Only if the check is deep enough Yes, by construction
Risk Correlated failure when the check is deep and shared Ejecting on a client-caused 5xx spike
When you'd actually pick it Always, as the membership baseline Always, as the fast layer on top — they are complements, not alternatives
Depth Proves Misses Correlated-failure risk
TCP connect Port is bound Wedged workers, exhausted pools, every application error None
Static HTTP 200 Request path is alive Dependency failures, degraded performance None
Local deep check This instance can serve — pool, config, warm-up Shared-dependency failures (deliberately) Low
Full deep check The whole path works Nothing — and that is the problem High — one dependency can empty the fleet

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The three numbers that define behaviour.

Detection latency is interval × unhealthy_threshold, plus up to one interval of phase offset. AWS's ALB defaults — 30-second interval, 2 consecutive failures — give a worst case near 90 seconds, during which 1/n of traffic fails. That single multiplication is the most useful piece of arithmetic in this note, and it is the one people never do before an incident.

Probe load is n_backends × n_checkers / interval probes per second. It is negligible for a load balancer and decidedly not negligible for a service mesh, where every sidecar may check every endpoint: 500 pods checking 500 pods every 5 seconds is 50,000 probes per second of pure overhead. This is why meshes lean on passive detection and why active checking is usually centralised.

The panic threshold is the fail-open rule expressed as a fraction. Envoy's default is 50%: if more than half the hosts in a cluster are marked unhealthy, it disregards health status entirely and load balances across all of them. The reasoning is a probability argument — the chance that more than half your fleet died simultaneously is far lower than the chance that your health checker is wrong — and it converts the most dangerous failure mode in this note from a total outage into a degradation.

Jitter matters more than it looks. Without it, n backends started by the same deploy probe in lockstep, so a dependency's momentary slowness is sampled at exactly the same instant by everyone, maximising correlation. Randomising the first probe offset decorrelates the sampling and is free.

7. Why It Matters in Production

Health checks decide the candidate set that every load balancing algorithm draws from, so they sit upstream of every other decision in this section. A perfect algorithm over a wrong candidate set produces perfectly balanced failure.

The observable is healthy-host-count as a fraction of fleet size, and the alert that matters is on correlation, not on individual ejections. One backend out of fifty is routine; twenty out of fifty within one interval is a health-check problem, and the distinction is the difference between an autoscaler event and an outage.

The second observable is the flat error floor. A shallow check that leaves one broken backend in rotation produces an error rate that sits at almost exactly 1/n of traffic and does not move with load. That flatness is diagnostic: real capacity problems scale with traffic, and a stuck fraction does not.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# Kubernetes: three probes, three different consequences
startupProbe:                       # covers a 3-minute model load
  httpGet: { path: /healthz/startup, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 40              # 40 x 5s = 200s budget before anything else runs
  periodSeconds: 5
readinessProbe:                     # gates traffic only - failure removes from endpoints
  httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8080 }   # LOCAL checks only: weights loaded, pool up
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 2               # out of rotation in ~10s
  successThreshold: 3               # slow to return: asymmetric on purpose
livenessProbe:                      # failure RESTARTS the pod - keep it shallow and slow
  httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 8080 }    # static 200; never touches dependencies
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 5               # ~100s of evidence before paying a 3-minute restart

# Envoy: active check plus the passive layer and the fail-open rule
health_checks:
- timeout: 2s
  interval: 10s                     # detection latency = 10s x 2 = ~20s
  unhealthy_threshold: 2
  healthy_threshold: 3
  http_health_check: { path: /healthz/ready }
outlier_detection:                  # passive: acts on real traffic in ~1 request
  consecutive_5xx: 5
  base_ejection_time: 30s
  max_ejection_percent: 50          # never eject more than half - the fail-open guard
common_lb_config:
  healthy_panic_threshold: { value: 50 }   # below 50% healthy, ignore health entirely

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Ten pods behind the Envoy config above. The shared database becomes slow at t=0 and recovers at t=30s.

🎬 t=0s    10/10 healthy. DB p99 jumps 5ms → 4000s-level stalls
    │      (readiness is LOCAL, so it does NOT observe the DB — by design)
    ▼
📥 [1] t=0–2s  real requests start timing out at the app layer
    │
    ▼
🔍 [2] t=2s   outlier detection sees consecutive_5xx on pods handling DB-backed routes
    │      ejects pods 1, 3, 7 → 7/10 healthy
    ▼
⚠️ [3] t=4s   failures continue on remaining pods; ejections reach 5/10
    │      max_ejection_percent: 50 reached → NO further ejections permitted
    ▼
🛡️ [4] t=6s   healthy fraction hits the 50% panic threshold
    │      Envoy DISREGARDS health status, balances across all 10
    │      → cached and non-DB routes keep succeeding
    ▼
🔧 [5] t=30s  DB recovers. Requests succeed again.
    │
    ▼
♻️ [6] t=30–60s  base_ejection_time 30s expires per pod, staggered by ejection time
    │      pods return gradually, NOT all at once → no herd against the fresh DB
    ▼
✅ [7] t=62s  10/10 healthy. Peak impact: DB-backed routes only, never a 503 floor

  1. Readiness never fired, and that is the design working. A readiness probe that pinged the database would have failed on all ten pods within one interval and handed the balancer an empty target group — converting a partial degradation into a total outage. Excluding shared dependencies from active checks is the single highest-leverage rule in this note.

  2. Outlier detection reacted in ~2 seconds, not ~20. Active checking with a 10s interval and threshold 2 would have needed 20 seconds to notice anything. Passive detection reused traffic that was already failing, which is why the two layers are complements: passive is fast and needs traffic, active is slow and does not.

  3. max_ejection_percent: 50 stopped the ejection cascade. Without it, all ten pods would have been ejected one after another as each accumulated its five consecutive failures, and the last ejection would have left zero targets.

  4. The panic threshold turned "no healthy hosts" into "ignore health". This is the fail-open behaviour, and it is the difference between serving degraded and serving 503. Note that it fired at 50% healthy — the balancer did not wait for zero, because by then it is already an outage.

  5. Staggered return prevented the recovery herd. Because pods were ejected at different times, their 30-second ejection timers expired at different times. Simultaneous re-admission of a whole fleet against a just-recovered dependency is the classic second failure, and jittered timing is what avoids it.

10. When TO Use This

  • Active checks as the membership baseline, always. They are the only signal available for a backend receiving no traffic — a newly started pod, a low-traffic region, a canary.

  • Passive outlier detection layered on top, always. It detects real failure in one request rather than in interval × threshold, and it catches "responds but wrongly", which no active check on a synthetic endpoint can see.

  • Deep checks scoped to local state. Verify what is true of this instance — pool initialised, config parsed, weights loaded, disk writable — and nothing shared.

  • Startup probes wherever warm-up is slow. Model loading, JIT warm-up and large cache hydration all need a probe that says "not yet" without implying "restart me".

  • Fail-open above a panic threshold, without exception. Below some healthy fraction, the checker is more likely wrong than the fleet.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not check shared dependencies in a per-instance health check. It converts a dependency degradation into a fleet-wide ejection. If the database is down, removing your backends from rotation helps nobody and removes the ones that could still serve cached responses.

  • Do not use TCP-connect checks for HTTP services. They pass while every request fails, producing the flat 1/n error floor that nothing on your dashboard explains. This is the most common shallow-check regression, and it usually arrives as a one-line change from ALB to NLB.

  • Do not tighten thresholds to detect faster without adding jitter and a panic threshold. Fast detection with correlated probes is a mechanism for amplifying a small blip into a fleet ejection.

  • Do not make liveness probes deep. Liveness failure restarts the process; a deep liveness probe means a dependency blip restarts your entire fleet, discarding every warm cache and in-flight request, and then all of them start cold at once.

  • Do not run active checks from every peer in a large mesh. n² probing is real load; centralise checking or lean on passive detection past a few hundred endpoints.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A deeper health check is a better health check."

✅ Reality: Depth increases the correlation of failures. A check that touches a shared dependency will mark every instance unhealthy simultaneously, which is the one failure mode a load balancer cannot route around. Depth is good exactly up to the boundary of what is local to the instance.

❌ Misconception: "If all backends are unhealthy, the balancer should stop sending traffic."

✅ Reality: That guarantees a total outage. If 100% of backends look unhealthy, the most likely explanation is that the checker is wrong, so the correct behaviour is to disregard health and keep serving — fail open. Envoy's 50% panic threshold and the Builders' Library's fail-static guidance both encode this.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes are basically the same check with different names."

✅ Reality: Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only removes it from Service endpoints. Pointing liveness at the same deep endpoint as readiness means a slow dependency does not merely take pods out of rotation, it kills and restarts them — turning a recoverable degradation into a crash-loop that destroys warm state fleet-wide.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing health checks as monitoring. They are a control loop that changes routing, not a dashboard. Framing them as observability misses that a health check acts, and that a wrong one causes outages rather than merely reporting them.

Not doing the detection-latency arithmetic. interval × threshold is one multiplication and it is the number that says how long 1/n of your traffic fails. Quoting defaults without multiplying them is the difference between having configured a balancer and having read its documentation.

Omitting the fail-open case entirely. The question "what does your balancer do when zero targets are healthy?" has a correct answer, and most people have never thought about it. Raising fail-open or the panic threshold unprompted is the strongest single signal available on this topic.

Treating active and passive as alternatives. They cover different failures at different speeds and every serious deployment runs both. "We use health checks" without distinguishing them is a shallow answer that the next question will expose.

Stopping at detection and never discussing recovery. The recovery herd — every backend returning at once against a dependency that has just recovered — causes the second outage, and staggering or jittering re-admission is the fix. An answer that ends at ejection has covered half the loop.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
ALB health check default interval 30 s With threshold 2, worst-case detection ~90 s AWS: ALB target group health checks
ALB health check default timeout 5 s Must stay well below the interval AWS: ALB target group health checks
ALB unhealthy / healthy thresholds 2 / 5 by default Deliberately asymmetric — quick out, slow back AWS: ALB target group health checks
Envoy healthy_panic_threshold 50% Below this, health status is disregarded entirely Envoy: Health checking
Envoy base_ejection_time default 30 s Multiplied by consecutive ejections Envoy: Outlier detection
Detection latency formula interval × unhealthy_threshold The one calculation to do before an incident, not during Derived from the above

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency Detection speed versus false ejections: every second cut from detection buys sensitivity to GC pauses and transient blips
💰 Cost Probe traffic is free at a balancer and O(n²) in a mesh; deep checks also cost the dependency they probe, at fleet scale
🔒 Security / visibility Health endpoints leak internal state and dependency topology — they belong on an internal port, never the public listener
📈 Scale Correlated failure risk grows with check depth, not with fleet size; a deep check is equally dangerous at 5 and 500 backends
🔧 Ops complexity Three probe types, two check styles and a panic threshold is a lot of surface — and every default is wrong for slow-starting workloads
🐛 Debuggability A shallow check produces a flat 1/n error floor with no failing component to point at; the balancer reports everything healthy while users see errors

16. Real World Usage

The Amazon Builders' Library article exists because of the correlated-failure mode. Its central guidance — prefer local checks, fail static when the unhealthy fraction is implausible, and be wary of health checks that depend on things outside the instance — is drawn from operating balancers at a scale where the failure mode is not hypothetical.

Envoy ships the panic threshold on by default at 50%. That is a strong statement from the reference L7 proxy: the designers judged that "more than half unhealthy" is more likely to be a checker fault than a fleet fault, and made ignoring health the default behaviour in that regime.

Kubernetes' three-probe split is a direct encoding of this note. Startup for warm-up, readiness for traffic gating, liveness for restart — three signals with three consequences, precisely because collapsing them causes the crash-loop and the empty-endpoints failures described above. The gRPC probe support added in 1.24 exists for the same reason: a TCP check against a gRPC server proves nothing.

17. Acronym Decoder

Topic name is not an acronym.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 109-load-balancing-algorithms.md — health checks define the candidate set every algorithm selects from

  • 108-l4-vs-l7.md — check depth is one of the table's most consequential rows

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 113-outlier-detection-circuit-breaking.md — the passive half, plus draining and graceful shutdown

  • 115-global-load-balancing.md — health-based routing across regions, where correlated failure spans continents

  • 07-http-semantics/59-status-codes.md — why an empty target group produces 503 and not 502

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Client-side health tracking — the caller keeps its own per-endpoint failure state instead of trusting a balancer (Item 114)

  • Queue-based work distribution — workers pull only when able, so health is implicit and needs no probing

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Connection draining — what makes an intentional ejection graceful rather than abrupt (Item 113)

  • Autoscaling — readiness gates whether new capacity actually receives traffic

  • Slow start — the ramp applied to a backend that has just become healthy (Item 109)

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Usually as an escalation from a load balancing question: "and how does the balancer know which backends are healthy?" The scenario that follows is almost always the correlated one — a shared dependency degrades, and the reviewer wants to know whether your design turns that into an outage. The strongest answers get to fail-open and local-only checks without being prompted, then name the recovery herd as the second-order problem.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (500 backends) Probe volume from multiple balancer nodes; correlated probe timing Jitter probe offsets; centralise active checking rather than per-proxy
100× (5,000 backends, meshed) n² probing between sidecars becomes real traffic and real CPU Lean on passive outlier detection; control-plane-driven health rather than peer probing
1000× (multi-region) Health signal propagation delay exceeds failure duration; regional correlation Health-based DNS or anycast failover with hysteresis; regional fail-open before global

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: synchronised probing. All backends probe a dependency on the same second, so a 200ms blip is sampled by everyone at once and the ejection is fleet-wide.

  • 100×: probe overhead in a mesh becomes a measurable fraction of request traffic, and the control plane's health propagation lags real state.

  • Operational: a health endpoint that quietly starts touching a new dependency because someone added a client library to the shared framework. Nothing in the config changed; the correlation risk appeared anyway.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Healthy host count as a fraction of fleet size, alerting on rate of change rather than level. A drop of more than 20% within one interval is a health-check event; a slow drift is an autoscaling one.

  • Ejections per minute, split active versus passive. Divergence tells you which layer is reacting, and a passive-only spike usually means a bad deploy rather than a bad dependency.

  • Time from container start to first successful request. The honesty check on your startup probe budget; drift here predicts the next launch failure.

  • 5xx composition at the balancer. A rising 503 share specifically means "no healthy targets" and points here, not at the application.

notes.title: Outlier Detection, Circuit Breaking, Draining & Graceful Shutdown

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Envoy calls it circuit breaking, but it isn't Hystrix's open/half-open state machine. What is it?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
How aggressive should outlier ejection be, and what stops it from ejecting the fleet?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Passive ejection on real traffic — Envoy: Outlier detection

  • Circuit breaking as concurrency limits, not a state machine — Envoy: Circuit breaking

  • Connection draining on a managed balancer — AWS: Target groups for your Application Load Balancers

  • Bonus — Amazon Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Outlier detection vs circuit breaking? Outlier ejects a bad backend. Circuit breaking caps load on all of them.
What does Envoy's circuit breaker actually do? Enforces concurrency limits — max connections, pending requests, retries — and fails fast past them.
What is deregistration delay for? Draining: finish in-flight requests on a target before removing it. AWS default is 300 s.
What does a pod need for graceful shutdown? Fail readiness first, keep serving through the drain, then exit — SIGTERM alone is not enough.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

These are the four mechanisms that decide what happens to traffic aimed at a backend that is failing, overloaded, or leaving. Outlier detection watches real request outcomes and ejects the backend that is misbehaving. Circuit breaking caps how much concurrent work may be outstanding to a cluster and fails fast beyond it, so a slow dependency cannot consume all your threads. Connection draining stops sending new work to a target while letting in-flight requests finish. Graceful shutdown is the backend's half of that contract — and it starts by failing readiness, not by exiting.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Envoy calls it circuit breaking, but it isn't Hystrix's open/half-open state machine. What is it?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know the term names two different mechanisms and can say which one you mean.

Envoy's circuit breakers are concurrency limits enforced at the connection pool: maximum connections, maximum pending requests, maximum active requests and maximum active retries, configured per cluster and per priority. When a limit is reached, further requests are rejected immediately with a local 503 rather than queued. There is no timed "open" state and no half-open probing — the breaker closes again the instant outstanding work drops below the limit.

The classical breaker, the one Fowler describes, is a state machine keyed on failure rate: after k failures it opens, rejects everything for a cooldown, then admits a trial request in half-open state and closes on success. Envoy achieves something close to that effect through outlier detection instead — a host ejected for consecutive 5xx is out for base_ejection_time, returns automatically, and is ejected again for longer if it fails again, which is the half-open trial in a different shape.

The reason the concurrency-limit form is preferred in a proxy is that it fails fast on overload, which is the more common production failure than hard errors. A dependency that is slow rather than broken will not trip a failure-rate breaker at all, but it will saturate a concurrency limit immediately.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

How aggressive should outlier ejection be, and what stops it from ejecting the fleet?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up whenever someone proposes passive health checking.

🎯 Really testing: whether you realise that the failure being detected is often not the backend's fault.

Aggressive ejection detects a genuinely broken instance in a single request, which is a large win over active checking's interval × threshold seconds. The risk is that outlier detection cannot distinguish "this backend is broken" from "this backend received the poison request" or "the shared dependency behind all backends is failing". A client sending malformed input that reliably produces a 500 will walk through your fleet ejecting every instance it touches.

The guard is max_ejection_percent, which caps the fraction of hosts that may be ejected at once — 50% is a sane setting and pairs with the panic threshold so that mass failure means "ignore health" rather than "serve nothing". The second guard is what you count: consecutive 5xx is noisy because it includes application errors, while consecutive gateway failures (connect errors, timeouts) counts only failures the backend is unambiguously responsible for. Counting the narrow signal and capping the ejection fraction gives you fast detection without fleet-wide risk.

My default is consecutive gateway failures of 5, a 30-second base ejection time with the standard multiplier for repeat offenders, and max_ejection_percent at 50 — then rely on active checks for the slow, membership-level truth underneath.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Mechanism Protects against Acts on Failure signal When you'd actually pick it
Outlier detection One bad instance A single backend Consecutive 5xx / gateway failures Always — the fast layer above active checks
Circuit breaking (concurrency) Overload and slow dependencies A whole upstream cluster Outstanding requests past a limit Always — it bounds resource consumption
Circuit breaking (state machine) A dependency that is hard-down A whole dependency Failure rate over a window In the client library, when the call is optional and degradable
Connection draining Killing in-flight requests A target being removed Deliberate — deploy or scale-in Every deploy; it is the difference between zero-downtime and not
Graceful shutdown The backend's side of draining The process itself SIGTERM Every service; readiness must fail before the process stops accepting

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The ordering is the entire mechanism, and it is where implementations go wrong. A process that exits on SIGTERM leaves the balancer still routing to it for however long its health-check or endpoint propagation takes — seconds during which a share of traffic hits a closed socket and clients see resets rather than a clean response. The correct sequence is: fail readiness, wait long enough for the balancer to observe it and for endpoint propagation to complete, keep serving throughout, then stop accepting and drain in-flight work, then exit.

The arithmetic that matters: the drain window must exceed endpoint propagation delay plus the longest in-flight request. Kubernetes propagation is typically a few seconds; an ALB's default deregistration delay is 300 seconds, which is generous for APIs and insufficient for long-lived streams that can outlive it. For a streaming service the drain window and the maximum stream duration are the same number, and if terminationGracePeriodSeconds is shorter than the drain, the orchestrator sends SIGKILL mid-drain and undoes all of it.

For outlier detection, the ejection duration is base_ejection_time × consecutive_ejection_count, so a repeatedly failing host is removed for progressively longer — 30s, 60s, 90s — which is the automatic backoff that stops a flapping instance from re-entering rotation every thirty seconds forever.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not eject on consecutive 5xx alone in a service with legitimate 5xx. Application errors caused by bad input are not backend faults; counting gateway failures instead confines ejection to failures the instance is genuinely responsible for.

  • Do not set circuit-breaker concurrency limits above what the backend can actually handle. A limit that is never reached provides no protection; the point is to fail fast at the proxy rather than queue unboundedly and convert an overload into a timeout cascade.

  • Do not rely on SIGTERM handling alone for zero-downtime deploys. Without failing readiness first and waiting out propagation, a perfectly implemented graceful shutdown still drops requests, because the balancer had not yet learned to stop sending them.

  • Do not set terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than the drain window. The orchestrator will SIGKILL the process partway through draining, which is indistinguishable from having no drain at all.

  • Do not use a state-machine circuit breaker on a call you cannot degrade. Opening the breaker means failing fast — that is only an improvement if the caller has something better to do than wait, such as a cached value or a reduced response.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Circuit breaking and outlier detection are the same thing."

✅ Reality: Outlier detection removes one bad host from the pool while the rest keep serving. Circuit breaking caps the load sent to the whole cluster and rejects the excess. One is a routing decision, the other is an admission decision, and a system usually needs both.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Kubernetes handles graceful shutdown for me — I just need to catch SIGTERM."

✅ Reality: SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen concurrently, not in order. If the process stops accepting connections immediately on SIGTERM, requests routed during the propagation window are reset. The pod must keep serving after SIGTERM — failing readiness, sleeping through propagation, then draining — which feels wrong the first time you write it.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 07-http-semantics/68-timeouts-retries-backoff.md — the client-side discipline these mechanisms complement

  • 109-load-balancing-algorithms.md — slow start, which is the mirror image of draining on the way in

  • 118-service-mesh.md — where these four mechanisms are configured per-service as policy

  • 13-kubernetes-networking/ rollout notes — how draining interacts with long-lived connections during a deploy

📚 Reference Links

  • The problem and the three families of solution — gRPC blog: gRPC Load Balancing

  • Why one connection carries everything — gRPC blog: gRPC on HTTP/2

  • Client-side balancing policies — gRPC: Custom Load Balancing Policies

  • Why a Kubernetes Service does not fix it — Kubernetes: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

  • Bonus — Envoy: Supported load balancers

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
One sentence: what is the problem? HTTP/2 multiplexes over one long-lived connection, and L4 balances connections — so all requests pin to one backend.
Why doesn't a Kubernetes Service fix it? kube-proxy is L4: it picks a pod at connection setup and never again.
The three solutions? An L7 proxy that speaks HTTP/2, client-side balancing with a resolver, or forcing connection cycling.
What symptom does it produce? One pod at 100% while the rest idle; scaling out does nothing to p99.
Which gRPC setting cycles connections? MAX_CONNECTION_AGE (server-side), which sends GOAWAY and forces a re-resolve.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which multiplexes every request over one long-lived TCP connection. An L4 balancer — an NLB, or kube-proxy behind a ClusterIP — chooses a backend once, at the SYN, and every request on that connection goes there for its whole life. So five client pods talking to forty server pods produce five busy pods and thirty-five idle ones, and adding capacity changes nothing. The fixes are an L7 proxy that balances per request, client-side balancing where the caller resolves all endpoints itself, or forcing connections to cycle with a max connection age.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why doesn't HTTP/1.1 have this problem?

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand that the problem is created by multiplexing, not by gRPC.

HTTP/1.1 has no multiplexing: one connection carries one request at a time. To get concurrency, a client opens a pool of connections — browsers historically six per origin, service clients typically tens to hundreds. Each of those connections is balanced independently, so an L4 hop with a pool of a hundred connections is making a hundred decisions, and balls-in-bins gets you acceptable distribution across a modest fleet.

HTTP/2 deliberately removes that: one connection, many concurrent streams, because opening connections is expensive and head-of-line blocking at the application layer was the thing it set out to fix. The consequence is that connection count collapses from hundreds to one, and connection count was exactly what the L4 balancer was distributing. The protocol improvement and the balancing regression are the same change viewed from two layers.

The problem is therefore not specific to gRPC. Any multiplexed client with connection reuse hits it; gRPC is simply the most common one in service architectures, so it wears the name.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Proxy-based or client-side load balancing?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up once you have named the problem; the gRPC project's own guidance frames it exactly this way.

🎯 Really testing: whether you weigh the extra hop against operational ownership, rather than picking the one you have read about.

Proxy-based means putting an L7 hop that speaks HTTP/2 between client and servers — Envoy, an ingress controller, a mesh sidecar. The client keeps one simple connection to the proxy, the proxy holds connections to every backend and dispatches per request. The advantages are that clients stay dumb and language-agnostic, policy lives in one place, and you get retries, outlier detection and observability for free. The costs are a hop of added latency, a component to operate and scale, and — for a shared proxy tier — a failure domain shared across services.

Client-side means the caller resolves all backend endpoints itself (through DNS, xDS, or a service registry) and runs the balancing algorithm locally, opening a connection to each. No extra hop, minimal latency, no shared failure domain. The costs are real: every client language needs a competent implementation, load-balancing policy is now deployed by upgrading clients rather than by changing config, and every client holds n connections, so a fleet of m clients and n servers has m × n connections to manage.

The tipping point I use is who owns the clients. If they are all yours, in one or two languages, with a mesh or xDS already in place, client-side (or sidecar-based, which is client-side with the implementation factored out) is excellent. If clients are heterogeneous, external, or owned by teams you cannot upgrade in lockstep, a proxy is the only maintainable answer — and the sidecar model is the popular compromise precisely because it gives client-side behaviour with proxy-style operations.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You fix it with MAX_CONNECTION_AGE. What breaks at 100× scale?

📍 Seen in the wild: the "we solved it with connection cycling" claim, examined.

Reconnect storms, and they synchronise. MAX_CONNECTION_AGE makes the server send GOAWAY after a fixed lifetime; the client finishes in-flight streams, re-resolves, and opens a new connection — which usually lands somewhere new, restoring distribution. At small scale this is elegant. At 10,000 clients with a 30-minute age, you have ~5.5 reconnects per second on average, which is fine — until a deploy starts every server pod within the same minute, at which point all their connection ages expire together and 10,000 clients reconnect within a few seconds of each other.

It presents as a periodic latency spike on a suspiciously round schedule, plus a CPU sawtooth on the server fleet from TLS handshakes, and a matching burst of DNS queries that can push a resolver into rate limiting. Each reconnect also costs a fresh TLS handshake and a cold HTTP/2 flow-control window, so p99 rises for the affected requests even when nothing fails. The mitigation is MAX_CONNECTION_AGE_GRACE plus jitter — gRPC adds a random component to the age precisely for this reason — and staggering server start times so ages do not align. The deeper point to make out loud: connection cycling is a mitigation that restores statistical balance over time, not a mechanism that balances requests. It converts a permanent skew into a periodically-corrected one, and if your request distribution matters within a 30-minute window, it is not a fix.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the traffic path for a model-serving fleet: a handful of gateway pods calling forty GPU inference pods over gRPC, with 10× request-cost variance.

📍 Seen in the wild: the AI-infrastructure form of this entire section.

🎯 Really testing: whether you connect the pinning problem to the cost of the underutilised resource — and GPUs are the most expensive idle resource in the estate.

The constraint that dominates is not latency, it is utilisation of a scarce, expensive resource. With a handful of gateway pods and an L4 hop, most of forty GPUs receive nothing; that is not a performance regression, it is most of the bill. So the requirement is per-request distribution, and the only question is where the L7 decision happens.

I would put an Envoy-based hop in the path that speaks HTTP/2 to the backends — either a sidecar on the gateway pods or a dedicated inference-routing tier — configured with least request and power-of-two-choices, not round robin, because 10× cost variance makes turn-order balancing produce queueing on unlucky pods (Item 109). Backends must be addressed as individual endpoints, not through a ClusterIP: a headless Service or an EndpointSlice-aware controller, so the proxy holds one HTTP/2 connection per pod and can dispatch across all of them. Slow start on newly-ready pods matters more than usual here, because a cold GPU pod with no in-flight requests is maximally attractive to least request and least able to serve.

The failure mode I would monitor first is max-to-median in-flight requests per pod, alerting above 1.5. It is the metric that directly detects the pinning problem, it is not on any default dashboard, and it regresses silently the moment someone puts a "simpler" L4 Service in front of the fleet. Second is GPU utilisation variance across pods, which is the same signal expressed in money. Third is reconnect rate, to catch a connection-cycling mitigation that has started to synchronise. The KV-cache- and queue-depth-aware routing that goes beyond this — routing by what the model server reports about its own state — belongs in the LLM serving folder; the wire-level fix stops here.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Solution Where the decision happens Latency cost Client changes Failure domain When you'd actually pick it
L7 proxy (Envoy, ingress, mesh gateway) A shared hop One extra hop None Shared tier Heterogeneous or external clients; you want one policy point
Sidecar proxy (mesh) Per-pod proxy Loopback only None Per-pod You already run a mesh; the common enterprise answer
Client-side (gRPC round_robin + headless Service) In the caller None Library config Per-client All clients are yours, in one or two languages
xDS / lookaside balancer Control plane informs the client None on the data path Library support Control plane Large fleets needing centralised policy without a data-path hop
MAX_CONNECTION_AGE cycling Nowhere — it just re-rolls the dice Reconnect cost, periodic Server config only None A mitigation when you cannot change the path; not a fix

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic of the skew. With c client connections spread over n backends by a hash, the distribution is balls-in-bins. At c = n the expected fraction of backends receiving zero connections is (1 − 1/n)^c → 1/e ≈ 37%. At c = 5, n = 40 — the shape in the Tier 4 question — the expected number of pods receiving at least one connection is at most 5, so at least 87.5% of the fleet is idle by construction, no matter which hash or algorithm the L4 hop uses. This is not a tuning problem; it is arithmetic, and saying it as arithmetic is what makes the point land.

Why L7 fixes it. An L7 hop that speaks HTTP/2 terminates the client's connection and maintains its own connections to every backend. Each request is a stream it can place on any of them, so the number of balancing decisions goes from c to r, the request count. Since r ≫ c for any multiplexed client, relative skew falls from the balls-in-bins bound to roughly 1/√r — which is the same inequality that underwrites Item 108's whole table.

Why connection cycling only half fixes it. MAX_CONNECTION_AGE re-rolls the assignment every T seconds. Over many cycles the time-averaged load evens out, but at any instant the distribution is still the balls-in-bins one. If your workload is bursty relative to T, or the resource being wasted is expensive per second (a GPU), time-averaged fairness is not the property you needed.

The connection-count cost of client-side balancing. m clients each holding a connection to n servers is m × n connections, and each carries HTTP/2 state, flow-control windows and keepalive timers. At m = 200, n = 100 that is 20,000 connections and the ceiling becomes file descriptors and memory on the server side — a different scaling problem traded for the balancing one.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This failure does not look like a failure. Every health check passes, every request succeeds, error rates are zero, and the only symptom is that p99 will not come down and the fleet is expensive. Teams respond by scaling out, which adds pods that receive no traffic, which makes the utilisation graph worse while the bill grows — and the load balancer is behaving exactly as documented the entire time.

The observable is max-to-median requests (or in-flight requests) per backend, and its cousin, the distribution of CPU or GPU utilisation across pods. A healthy L7-balanced fleet sits near 1.1; a pinned gRPC fleet routinely exceeds 3, and in the small-client case can be effectively unbounded, with most pods at zero.

For AI systems the money version is the one that lands. Idle CPU pods waste cents; idle GPU pods waste dollars per hour each, and a forty-pod fleet with five effective pods runs at 12% utilisation of its most expensive resource. Utilisation of the scarce resource, not latency, is what makes this a first-order architecture concern.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

# WRONG: ClusterIP Service - kube-proxy is L4, so gRPC pins to one pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: inference }
spec:
  type: ClusterIP              # a single virtual IP; one conntrack entry per connection
  selector: { app: inference }
  ports: [{ port: 50051 }]
---
# RIGHT (client-side): headless Service exposes every pod IP via DNS
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: inference-headless }
spec:
  clusterIP: None              # DNS returns ALL pod IPs, not one VIP
  selector: { app: inference }
  ports: [{ port: 50051 }]

// Client side: resolve every endpoint and balance across them in the caller
conn, err := grpc.NewClient(
    "dns:///inference-headless.default.svc.cluster.local:50051", // all pod IPs
    grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(`{"loadBalancingConfig":[{"round_robin":{}}]}`),
)

// Server side: the mitigation, when you cannot change the path
srv := grpc.NewServer(grpc.KeepaliveParams(keepalive.ServerParameters{
    MaxConnectionAge:      30 * time.Minute, // gRPC adds jitter to this internally
    MaxConnectionAgeGrace: 30 * time.Second, // let in-flight streams finish after GOAWAY
}))

9. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Five gateway pods, forty inference pods, ~2,000 requests/second, behind the ClusterIP Service above.

🎬 t=0     5 gateway pods start; each dials inference:50051 once
    │
    ▼
⚖️ [1] kube-proxy picks a pod per connection (random among 40)
    │   result: pods {7, 7, 19, 31, 33} chosen — pod 7 twice by chance
    │   → 4 distinct pods serving, 36 idle
    ▼
📡 [2] each connection carries ~400 req/s over multiplexed streams
    │   pod 7: ~800 req/s | pods 19,31,33: ~400 req/s | pods 1-6,8-18,20-30,32,34-40: 0
    ▼
📊 [3] observed: max/median in-flight = ∞ (median is 0), GPU util 4/40 pods
    │   dashboards: error rate 0.0%, all 40 targets HEALTHY ✅
    ▼
🔧 [4] response: scale to 60 pods  → still 4 serving, 56 idle. p99 unchanged.
    │
    ▼
✅ [5] fix: headless Service + round_robin in the client
    │   5 clients × 40 connections = 200 connections; every pod receives ~50 req/s
    ▼
📊 [6] observed after: max/median in-flight ≈ 1.15, GPU util even across 40 pods

  1. Step 1 is the whole bug, and it takes one packet. The SYN is the only moment a balancing decision is made. Everything after it is a conntrack lookup, and 20,000 requests inherit a choice made once.

  2. Pod 7 was chosen twice by chance, and that is expected. With 5 balls in 40 bins, collisions are ordinary; the balls-in-bins distribution does not care that you wanted spread. This is why "use a better hash" is not a fix.

  3. Every dashboard was green. Zero errors, forty healthy targets, latency merely mediocre. The only signals that name the problem are per-pod request distribution and per-pod resource utilisation, and neither is on a default dashboard. This is the practical lesson of the note.

  4. Scaling out made it worse. Twenty more pods, zero additional traffic served, twenty more GPUs billed. Any time adding capacity does not move p99, distribution — not capacity — is the constraint.

  5. The fix multiplied connections by 40 and that is the trade. 200 connections instead of 5, each with its own HTTP/2 state and keepalives. At this size it is free; at 500 clients it becomes the next scaling conversation, which is when a sidecar or an L7 tier starts to look better than client-side.

10. When TO Use This

(This note is a failure mode, so "when to use" is read as: when to apply each remedy.)

  • L7 proxy tier — when clients are heterogeneous, external, or not yours to upgrade. One policy point, no client changes, and you inherit retries and outlier detection with it.

  • Sidecar / mesh — when you already run a mesh, or when per-pod blast radius matters. It is client-side balancing with the implementation factored out of your application code, which is why it is the common enterprise answer.

  • Client-side balancing — when all clients are yours, in one or two languages, and the extra hop's latency genuinely matters. Pair it with a headless Service so DNS returns every endpoint.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not put a plain L4 Service or NLB in front of an HTTP/2 backend fleet and expect distribution. This is the whole note. If the path must be L4 for another reason, you need one of the remedies above alongside it, not instead of a diagnosis.

  • Do not choose client-side balancing when m × n connection count is already large. Two hundred clients against a hundred servers is 20,000 connections of HTTP/2 state; you have swapped a distribution problem for a file-descriptor and memory problem.

  • Do not treat connection cycling as the fix on a latency-sensitive or cost-sensitive path. It restores balance on average over the cycle window, and it costs a TLS handshake and a cold flow-control window every time it fires.

  • Scale limit to name: the L7 remedy is bounded by per-request state at the proxy; the client-side remedy is bounded by m × n connections. Neither is fixable by choosing bigger instances, and the crossover is where sidecars win.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "This is a gRPC problem."

✅ Reality: It is an HTTP/2-plus-connection-reuse problem. Any multiplexed, long-lived client hits it. gRPC is simply the most common one in service architectures, and the one whose documentation says so most clearly.

❌ Misconception: "A Kubernetes Service load balances my pods."

✅ Reality: kube-proxy balances connections by writing a DNAT rule at connection setup. It has no notion of a request and never revisits the choice. For HTTP/1.1 with a connection pool this is adequate; for HTTP/2 it is a single decision that governs the connection's whole life.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Switching the load balancing algorithm from round robin to least connections will fix the skew."

✅ Reality: Both are connection-level algorithms, and with five connections there is nothing to distribute — the algorithm is being asked to spread five things over forty and is doing that correctly. No algorithm change helps, because the unit being balanced is wrong. Only moving the decision to L7 or into the client changes the unit.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Describing the symptom without naming the unit. "One pod is hot" is an observation; "the balancer is distributing connections, and HTTP/2 gave it one connection to distribute" is the diagnosis. The word unit — connections versus requests — is what makes the answer sound like experience rather than recall.

Presenting MAX_CONNECTION_AGE as a fix. It bounds the skew over time; it does not balance requests. Calling it a mitigation, unprompted, is a credibility marker — and it sets up the reconnect-storm discussion, which is the more interesting follow-up anyway.

Skipping the arithmetic. "Most pods get nothing" is vague. "Five connections over forty pods means at least 87.5% of the fleet is idle by construction" is checkable, memorable, and forecloses the "surely a better hash would help" objection before it is raised.

Stopping at the network layer on an AI question. For a model-serving fleet, the point is not latency but utilisation of an expensive scarce resource, and the routing conversation continues into queue-depth and cache-aware placement. Knowing where the wire-level answer ends and the serving-layer answer begins is itself the architect-level signal.

14. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Idle backends at c connections over n pods (1 − 1/n)^c At c=5, n=40: ≥87.5% idle by construction Balls-in-bins; direct calculation
Idle backends at c = n ~37% (1/e) The general L4 skew result Balls-in-bins, standard result
HTTP/2 default max concurrent streams Commonly 100–250 per connection, server-advertised Why one connection is enough for a client, and why the skew persists RFC 9113 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS
gRPC MaxConnectionAge No default — off unless set Jitter is applied by the implementation when it is set gRPC keepalive documentation
Healthy max/median in-flight per backend ~1.1–1.2 Alert above 1.5; a pinned fleet reads 3+ or unbounded Operational rule of thumb — measure yours
Connections under client-side LB m × n 200 clients × 100 servers = 20,000 Direct calculation

15. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
⏱️ Latency An L7 hop costs a fraction of a millisecond; the skew it removes costs queueing measured in tens or hundreds
💰 Cost The purest cost failure in this section: idle GPUs bill at full rate while dashboards report perfect health
🔒 Security / visibility Client-side balancing removes the central hop where mTLS, policy and per-request logs lived; a sidecar restores it
📈 Scale L7 scales with per-request state; client-side scales with m × n connections. The crossover is where meshes earn their complexity
🔧 Ops complexity Client-side moves policy into client releases — changing a balancing algorithm becomes a fleet-wide dependency upgrade
🐛 Debuggability The failure is invisible in every standard metric; you must add per-backend request distribution deliberately, before you need it

16. Real World Usage

The gRPC project documents this as a first-class concern, not a footnote — the load balancing post exists because the naive Kubernetes deployment is the common case and it silently does the wrong thing. Its framing of proxy versus client-side versus lookaside is the vocabulary most teams end up using.

Service meshes are in large part a productised answer to it. A sidecar gives every workload an L7 proxy on loopback, making per-request HTTP/2 balancing the default rather than something each client library must implement — one of the strongest arguments for a mesh in an internal-gRPC estate (Item 118).

Model-serving stacks hit it hardest. Inference gateways speak gRPC or HTTP/2, are called by few clients, and front the most expensive compute in the company. The guidance in serving frameworks — route by in-flight requests or queue depth, address pods individually — exists because the L4 default wastes accelerators at a rate nobody notices until the invoice arrives.

17. Acronym Decoder

  • gRPC — the acronym is recursive and teaches nothing about the mechanism; skipped per the decoder rule. What matters is that it is RPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf, and the HTTP/2 part is the entire subject of this note.

  • GOAWAY — not an acronym but the HTTP/2 frame that matters here: the server telling a client "finish your open streams, then reconnect", which is the mechanism behind connection cycling.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 06-http-versions/ HTTP/2 multiplexing — the feature that creates the problem

  • 106-l4-load-balancing.md — per-connection balancing, stated in general form

  • 108-l4-vs-l7.md — the table row this note is the worked example of

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 118-service-mesh.md — the sidecar remedy, and when it is worth its complexity

  • 117-ingress-controllers.md — the ingress-level remedy inside Kubernetes

  • 16-ai-networking/ inference routing — where request-aware routing continues past the wire

🔀 Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Lookaside / xDS balancing — a control plane tells clients where to send, keeping the data path direct

  • Queue-based dispatch — workers pull from a queue, which removes the balancing decision entirely

  • HTTP/1.1 with a connection pool — sidestepping the problem by giving up multiplexing, occasionally the right call for simple internal RPC

🧩 Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Least request with P2C — the algorithm the L7 remedy should use, given cost variance (Item 109)

  • Slow start — needed because newly-ready pods are maximally attractive to least request (Item 109)

  • Health checks — the candidate set the remedy distributes over (Item 112)

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

Almost always as a trap inside a larger design: you draw services talking gRPC through a Kubernetes Service, and the reviewer asks how traffic is distributed. The strong answer names the unit mismatch immediately, does the arithmetic, and then chooses a remedy with its trade-off stated. On an AI-platform design the follow-up is about GPU utilisation rather than latency, which is where the cost framing earns its place.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (50 clients, 400 backends) Client-side connection count reaches 20,000; server memory per connection becomes real Move to sidecar or a shared L7 tier so backends see one connection per proxy, not per client
100× (500 clients, multi-cluster) Endpoint discovery churn; DNS-based resolution can no longer keep up with pod turnover xDS control plane for endpoint distribution; EndpointSlice-aware routing
1000× (multi-region inference) Cross-region egress cost per request dominates; a global balancer cannot see per-pod load Region-local L7 routing with global routing only for failover; keep the per-request decision inside the region

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: connection state on the server side under client-side balancing — file descriptors, HTTP/2 window memory, and keepalive timer volume.

  • 100×: endpoint propagation lag. Pods churn faster than resolvers refresh, so clients balance across a stale endpoint set and send requests to addresses that no longer exist.

  • Operational: someone adds a "simpler" L4 Service in front of the working L7 path during an unrelated change. Nothing errors, distribution silently collapses, and the regression is invisible without the per-pod distribution metric.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Max-to-median in-flight requests per backend, alerting above 1.5. The direct detector for this failure and the single most valuable metric in this note.

  • Per-pod GPU or CPU utilisation variance across the fleet. The same signal in the currency that gets budget attention.

  • Connection count per backend, and reconnect rate. A backend with far more connections than its peers is the pinning problem; a fleet-wide reconnect spike is a synchronised MAX_CONNECTION_AGE.

  • Endpoint set size as seen by clients versus actual ready pods. Divergence means resolution is stale and the balancing algorithm is choosing from a fiction.

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Why is anycast failover faster than DNS failover?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Latency-based DNS routing or anycast for a multi-region API?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • DNS-based failover and its health model — AWS: Failover routing (Route 53)

  • How health status changes which record is returned — AWS: How Route 53 chooses records when health checking is configured

  • Latency-based routing — AWS: Values specific for latency records

  • Bonus — cloudflare.com/learning: What is a reverse proxy? (the anycast edge model in context)

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three mechanisms? DNS-based (return a different record), anycast (same IP announced from many PoPs), GSLB (DNS plus health and policy).
Why is DNS failover slow? Resolver and OS caches ignore your TTL floor; real failover is TTL plus stubborn caches, minutes not seconds.
What does anycast fail over on? BGP withdrawal — routes reconverge in seconds, with no client involvement at all.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

Global load balancing decides which region a client reaches, before any regional balancer sees the request. DNS-based routing answers the query differently per client — by latency, geography, weight or health — and is the most flexible, but it inherits DNS caching, so failover is measured in minutes and clients ignore your TTL. Anycast announces one IP address from many locations and lets BGP pick the nearest, so failover is a route withdrawal and takes seconds. GSLB is DNS with health checking and policy bolted on. The trap is treating DNS TTL as a control you actually have.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why is anycast failover faster than DNS failover?

Because nothing on the client side has to change. Under anycast, every region announces the same prefix via BGP, and each router forwards to the topologically nearest announcement. When a region fails, it withdraws the announcement; routers reconverge and traffic follows the next-nearest path within seconds. The client's DNS answer, its cached IP and its configuration are all still correct — only the network's opinion of where that IP lives has changed.

DNS failover has to reach every client through a chain of caches you do not control: the recursive resolver, the OS stub resolver, the browser's own cache, and any corporate resolver in between. Your record may carry a 60-second TTL and still be served from some resolver's cache for far longer, because TTL honouring is inconsistent in practice and some resolvers enforce their own minimum. The mechanism is fundamentally "wait for other people's caches to expire", which is why it is measured in minutes and why a small tail of clients persists for much longer.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Latency-based DNS routing or anycast for a multi-region API?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that anycast's weakness is statefulness, not speed.

Latency-based DNS gives you fine-grained, policy-driven control: weights for a gradual regional shift, geographic overrides for data-residency requirements, and per-record health checks. You can move 5% of Europe to a new region with a single change. The costs are cache-bound failover and the fact that the routing decision is made from the resolver's location, not the client's — so a client using a distant public resolver gets routed for where its resolver is.

Anycast is faster, needs no client cooperation and is the only practical way to absorb volumetric DDoS, because the traffic is spread across every PoP by the network itself. Its weakness is that route changes can move a client mid-session: BGP reconvergence during normal internet churn can shift a client to a different PoP, which is fatal for a long-lived TCP connection and merely annoying for stateless HTTP. That is why anycast is standard for DNS and CDN edges — where sessions are short or the edge terminates them — and rarer for direct-to-origin stateful services.

The common answer is both, layered: anycast to the CDN or edge tier for absorption and speed, DNS-based policy behind it for regional origin selection. The tipping point for using DNS alone is whether you need policy expressiveness (residency, weighted shifts) more than you need seconds-scale failover.

4. Quick Comparison Table

DNS-based routing Anycast GSLB (DNS + health + policy)
Failover speed Minutes — TTL plus stubborn caches Seconds — BGP reconvergence Minutes, same DNS constraint
Decision made from The resolver's location The network's topology Resolver location plus health state
Session stability Stable once resolved Can move mid-session on route change Stable once resolved
DDoS absorption None Excellent — spread across all PoPs None
Policy expressiveness High — weights, geo, latency Low — the network decides Highest
Operational requirement A DNS provider Your own ASN and BGP, or a provider's A GSLB product
When you'd actually pick it Weighted or residency-driven regional control Edge tiers, DNS, DDoS-exposed services Multi-region active-active with real health awareness

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic worth carrying: real failover time is TTL + resolver caching slack + client caching slack + detection time. Detection alone is a health-check interval times a threshold (Item 112) — Route 53's health checks report unhealthy after a few consecutive failures at a 30-second interval by default. Add a 60-second TTL and inconsistent honouring downstream, and a "60-second TTL" system realistically fails over most traffic in two to five minutes with a long tail. Planning a regional failover SLO tighter than that on DNS alone is planning on a mechanism that does not exist.

Anycast's equivalent is BGP convergence, typically seconds within a well-connected network and up to tens of seconds across the public internet — no client-side term in the equation at all, which is the whole difference.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not rely on DNS TTL as a failover control. Resolvers, operating systems and applications cache beyond your TTL, and some JVM and library defaults cache DNS answers for the process lifetime. If your recovery plan says "we drop the TTL to 30 seconds", it is a plan built on a number you do not control.

  • Do not use anycast for long-lived stateful connections to origin. A routing change mid-session lands the client on a PoP with no knowledge of it; for WebSocket or long streams this is a disconnect, not a rebalance.

  • Do not route by resolver geography when data residency is a legal requirement. The resolver's location is a proxy for the client's, and a wrong guess is a compliance incident rather than a latency regression. Residency needs an authoritative signal at the application layer.

  • Do not run active-active across regions without deciding what the data layer does. Global load balancing is the easy half; two regions writing to the same logical dataset is the hard half, and it is not a networking problem (see the HLD folder's replication notes).

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A 30-second TTL means we fail over in 30 seconds."

✅ Reality: TTL is a request, not a guarantee. Add health-check detection time, resolver caches that enforce their own minimums, OS and application-level caching, and the realistic figure is minutes with a tail of clients that persist far longer.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Latency-based routing measures the client's latency."

✅ Reality: The authoritative server sees the resolver's address, not the client's. A user on a distant public resolver is routed as if they were where that resolver is. EDNS Client Subnet mitigates this by passing a truncated client prefix, but it is not universally supported and not universally sent.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 04-dns/32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md — the caching chain that sets your real failover time

  • 04-dns/33-dns-load-balancing.md — the DNS mechanism this note extends to multi-region

  • 112-health-checks.md — health-based routing is health checking at continental scale

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 119-cdn-and-edge.md — the anycast edge tier in practice

  • 02-ip-packets-routing/ BGP and anycast notes — the routing layer underneath

  • Multi-region data replication in the HLD folder — the half of active-active that networking does not solve
