headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Where does the load balancer end and the gateway begin?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
A dedicated gateway tier, or push these concerns into the ingress controller?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Gateway-shaped features on a managed L7 balancer — AWS: Application Load Balancers

  • The proxy primitives a gateway is built from — Envoy: Life of a Request

  • Gateway vs ingress, as the Kubernetes API now models it — Gateway API: Introduction

  • Bonus — RFC 9110 §3.7: Intermediaries

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does a gateway have that a load balancer doesn't? Identity. Auth, per-tenant quota and transformation all need to know who is calling.
Gateway vs ingress? Ingress is Kubernetes' way of exposing a Service at L7; a gateway adds identity-aware policy on top.
The classic anti-pattern? Business logic in the gateway — orchestration, aggregation, field mapping that belongs in a service.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An API gateway is the hop that owns everything a request needs after it has been identified and before it becomes application logic: authentication and token validation, per-tenant rate limits and quotas, routing to the right service version, request and response transformation, and consistent observability. It is architecturally the same machinery as a reverse proxy — usually literally Envoy or nginx underneath — with one addition that changes its position in the stack: it knows who the caller is, and every policy it enforces is keyed on that identity rather than on an IP.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Where does the load balancer end and the gateway begin?

The dividing line is identity. A load balancer decides which instance should serve a request, using information available from the connection and the request line. A gateway decides whether this caller may make this request, at this rate, right now — which requires validating a credential and looking up an identity, something a balancer has no reason to do.

That difference explains the ordering. Authentication must happen before per-tenant rate limiting, because the limit is keyed on the tenant; rate limiting at the edge, before identity exists, can only key on IP, which over-limits corporate NAT and under-limits a distributed abuser. So the gateway sits behind the L7 balancer, not in front of it: the balancer gets the request to a healthy gateway instance, and the gateway applies identity-aware policy.

In practice the boundary blurs, because managed products cross it. An ALB with OIDC authentication and a WAF is doing gateway work; a Kong or Apigee deployment is doing balancer work. The useful test in a design discussion is not the product name but where identity is established, because that is the point after which per-tenant policy becomes possible.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

A dedicated gateway tier, or push these concerns into the ingress controller?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard follow-up on any Kubernetes platform design.

🎯 Really testing: whether you weigh the cost of an extra hop against the cost of an overloaded one.

Pushing gateway concerns into the ingress controller removes a hop and a component. Modern ingress controllers are Envoy or nginx with plugin systems, so JWT validation, rate limiting and header manipulation are all expressible there. For a single team with a handful of services, that is the right amount of machinery, and adding a separate gateway is architecture for its own sake.

A dedicated tier earns its place when the policy surface grows or the ownership splits. If a platform team owns the ingress and product teams own API policy, a shared ingress config becomes a contention point where one team's rate-limit change is deployed by another team's pipeline. A separate gateway gives product teams a policy surface they can move without touching cluster ingress, and it lets the gateway scale on a different curve — auth and quota work is CPU-heavy in a way that path routing is not.

My tipping point is whether more than one team needs to change policy independently, or whether the gateway needs stateful behaviour the ingress cannot hold — distributed quota counters, API key management, response caching keyed on identity. Below that, ingress plus a small auth filter is less machinery for the same result.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Load balancer (L7) API gateway Ingress controller Service mesh
Primary job Pick a healthy instance Enforce identity-aware policy Expose Services at L7 inside Kubernetes Service-to-service policy and mTLS
Knows the caller's identity No Yes — that is the point Only with an auth plugin Yes, as a workload identity
Traffic direction North–south North–south North–south East–west
Typical scope A fleet An API product A cluster A whole mesh
When you'd actually pick it Always, underneath everything External or multi-tenant APIs needing quota and auth Kubernetes-native L7 exposure Internal traffic policy at scale

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The ordering is forced the same way the reverse proxy's is: each stage needs what the previous one produced. Credential validation must precede authorisation, authorisation must precede quota (you cannot count per tenant before you know the tenant), and all of it must precede routing, because a rejected request should never cost a backend connection.

The one piece of math worth naming is distributed quota accounting. With g gateway instances and a per-tenant limit of L requests per window, each instance enforcing L/g locally is simple and wrong under uneven distribution — a tenant whose traffic lands mostly on one instance is limited at L/g while a well-spread tenant gets L. Shared counters in Redis give correctness at the cost of a network round trip on every request; the usual compromise is local counting with periodic reconciliation, which admits a bounded overshoot of roughly g × (sync interval × rate) requests. Stating that overshoot as a number is what turns "we rate limit" into a design answer.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not put business logic in the gateway. Response aggregation across services, field-level mapping and conditional orchestration all become a deployment bottleneck owned by a platform team, versioned separately from the services whose contracts they encode. This is the most expensive gateway mistake and it is always incremental.

  • Do not add a gateway when you have one team and five services. The ingress controller plus an auth filter does the same work with one fewer component and one fewer failure domain.

  • Do not use it for east–west traffic. Service-to-service policy through a central north–south hop adds a hop, a hairpin and a shared failure domain; that is what a mesh is for (Item 118).

  • Do not rely on per-instance rate limiting for a hard quota. Without shared counters the effective limit varies with how the balancer happened to distribute a tenant's traffic, which makes the limit unpredictable in exactly the case it exists for.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "An API gateway is a different kind of software from a reverse proxy."

✅ Reality: Most gateways are a reverse proxy — Envoy, nginx or similar — with an auth and policy layer on top. The distinction is where identity is established and what policy is keyed on, not the binary.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Rate limiting belongs at the edge, as far out as possible."

✅ Reality: Far out means before authentication, which means the only key available is the IP address. That over-limits every user behind a corporate NAT and barely inconveniences a distributed abuser. Volumetric protection belongs at the edge; quota belongs behind auth, where the tenant is known.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 105-reverse-proxy-responsibilities.md — the machinery a gateway is built from

  • 07-http-semantics/69-rate-limiting.md — the algorithm behind the quota stage

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 117-ingress-controllers.md — where these responsibilities land inside Kubernetes

  • 118-service-mesh.md — the east–west counterpart, and where the two overlap

  • 10-api-protocols/ webhook and async notes — the traffic shapes a gateway handles worst

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Trace the path of an external request to a pod through an Ingress.
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Stay on Ingress, or migrate to the Gateway API?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What an Ingress resource is, and is not — Kubernetes: Ingress

  • The controller half of the contract — Kubernetes: Ingress Controllers

  • The successor API and why it exists — Gateway API: Introduction

  • Bonus — Kubernetes: Virtual IPs and Service Proxies

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does the Ingress resource actually do? Nothing on its own. It is configuration that a controller must be running to act on.
Why did the Gateway API replace it? Ingress underspecified everything beyond host/path, so every feature became a vendor annotation.
What are the three Gateway API roles? GatewayClass (infra provider), Gateway (cluster operator), HTTPRoute (app developer).

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

An Ingress controller is a reverse proxy — usually NGINX, Traefik or Envoy — running inside the cluster, watching the Kubernetes API for Ingress resources and rewriting its own configuration to match. The Ingress resource itself does nothing; it is declarative config with no behaviour, and if no controller is installed it is inert. Its problem is that it standardised only host and path routing, so header matching, traffic splitting, timeouts and everything else became vendor-specific annotations. The Gateway API is the replacement: a typed, role-separated API where those features are first-class rather than strings in a metadata block.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Trace the path of an external request to a pod through an Ingress.

The external entry point is not the Ingress at all — it is a cloud load balancer pointing at the controller's own Service, usually of type LoadBalancer or NodePort. That balancer is L4 in the common case, and it distributes across the controller's replicas.

The controller pod receives the request, terminates TLS using a certificate from a Secret referenced by the Ingress, and matches host and path against the rules it has compiled from every Ingress resource in the cluster. Having chosen a backend Service, a well-implemented controller does not send the request to the Service's ClusterIP — it resolves the Service to its EndpointSlices and connects directly to a pod IP, so the L7 balancing decision is its own rather than kube-proxy's.

That last detail is the one worth knowing cold, because it is what makes the Ingress path an L7 path end to end. A controller that proxies to the ClusterIP instead reintroduces kube-proxy's per-connection L4 behaviour behind an L7 hop, which is exactly the pinning problem for HTTP/2 backends (Item 114).

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Stay on Ingress, or migrate to the Gateway API?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can evaluate an API migration on portability and role separation rather than on features alone.

Ingress works, is universally supported, and every controller understands it. Its failure is expressiveness: because the spec stops at host and path, everything else lives in annotations like nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering, which are per-controller strings with no schema, no validation and no portability. A cluster's routing behaviour ends up encoded in a vendor's annotation vocabulary, and switching controllers becomes a rewrite rather than a swap.

The Gateway API fixes this by typing the features — header and method matching, weighted traffic splitting, timeouts, request mirroring — and by splitting the API across three roles so that a platform team owns the Gateway and its TLS while application teams own their own HTTPRoutes without cluster-wide permissions. It also cleanly extends beyond HTTP to TCP, UDP and gRPC routes.

The cost is migration and maturity: two routing APIs in flight during the transition, controller support that varies by feature, and a team that has to learn a second model. My tipping point is whether annotation sprawl is already causing pain — multiple teams editing one Ingress, or a controller migration that has been deferred because the annotations are unportable. New clusters should start on the Gateway API; established ones should migrate when the annotation surface, not the feature list, becomes the problem.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Ingress Gateway API
Routing expressiveness Host and path only, in-spec Host, path, header, method, query; weighted splits; mirroring
Everything else Vendor annotations — unvalidated strings Typed fields with schema validation
Role separation None — one resource, one permission GatewayClass / Gateway / Route across three roles
Protocols HTTP(S) HTTP, gRPC, TLS, TCP, UDP routes
Portability between controllers Poor once annotations are used Good for in-spec features
When you'd actually pick it Existing clusters, simple host/path exposure New clusters, multi-team ownership, anything beyond basic routing

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The controller is a control loop, and the proxy is a data plane — the separation matters because their failure modes differ. If the controller dies, the proxy keeps serving the last configuration it was given: routing is frozen but traffic flows. If the proxy dies, everything stops. This is why controllers are deployed with multiple replicas and why "the ingress controller is unhealthy" needs a follow-up question about which half.

The scaling property to name is configuration size, not request rate. Every Ingress in the cluster compiles into one proxy configuration, so a cluster with thousands of Ingress objects produces a config file that takes seconds to generate and reload. Older nginx-based controllers reloaded the whole process on any change, which dropped or reset long-lived connections cluster-wide on an unrelated team's deploy; Envoy-based controllers push incremental updates over xDS instead, which is the main architectural reason for preferring them at scale.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not rely on Ingress annotations for anything you need portable. They are per-controller, unvalidated and silently ignored when misspelled — a mistyped buffering annotation does not error, it just leaves buffering on and breaks your streams.

  • Do not use a config-reloading controller for long-lived connections at scale. If a full reload resets connections, every unrelated Ingress change in the cluster becomes a disconnect event for your WebSocket or SSE users.

  • Do not put east–west traffic through the ingress. Service-to-service calls hairpinning out to the ingress and back add latency, a shared failure domain, and a bill for traffic that never needed to leave the cluster.

  • Do not treat the Ingress resource as the thing doing the work. Without a controller installed and running, an Ingress object is inert configuration — a surprisingly common cause of "I applied it and nothing happened".

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "Ingress is the Kubernetes load balancer."

✅ Reality: There are three distinct things — kube-proxy doing L4 balancing for Services, the cloud load balancer in front of the controller, and the controller's own L7 proxying. A request can pass through all three, and knowing which one made which decision is the whole of Kubernetes traffic debugging.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The Ingress controller sends traffic to the Service, so kube-proxy balances it."

✅ Reality: Good controllers resolve EndpointSlices and connect straight to pod IPs, bypassing kube-proxy entirely so the L7 decision is theirs. Controllers that do proxy to the ClusterIP reintroduce L4 per-connection pinning behind an L7 hop — the difference is invisible in config and decisive for HTTP/2 backends.

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
What changes on the wire when a sidecar is injected?
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
When is a mesh worth its complexity?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Sidecar versus sidecarless, from the reference implementation — Istio: Sidecar or ambient?

  • What the sidecarless data plane actually is — Istio: Ambient Mode overview

  • The proxy every mesh is built on — Envoy: Life of a Request

  • Bonus — Envoy: Outlier detection

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is the data plane? A proxy per workload (sidecar) or per node (ambient) that carries all service-to-service traffic.
What does it buy that a library cannot? Language-independent policy, deployed by config rather than by upgrading every client.
The honest cost? Latency per hop, a proxy's memory per pod, and a control plane that is now critical infrastructure.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A service mesh moves retries, timeouts, mTLS, traffic splitting, per-request load balancing and telemetry out of application code and into a proxy that intercepts every service-to-service call. In the sidecar model that proxy is a container in each pod; in the newer ambient or sidecarless model it is a per-node component with an optional per-namespace layer for L7 work. The payoff is uniform behaviour across languages, changed by configuration instead of by a fleet-wide library upgrade. The cost is a proxy hop on every internal call and a control plane that becomes critical infrastructure — which is why the real question is when it is worth its complexity.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

What changes on the wire when a sidecar is injected?

An init container or a CNI plugin installs redirection rules so that all inbound and outbound traffic for the pod passes through the sidecar's ports rather than going directly to the application. The application dials the same address it always did; the connection is intercepted locally and terminated by the proxy, which then opens its own connection to the destination's sidecar. So one logical call becomes client-app → client-sidecar → server-sidecar → server-app: two extra proxy hops, both over loopback or the pod network.

Those hops are where the features live. Because the sidecar terminates and re-originates, it can upgrade the connection to mTLS with a workload identity certificate rotated by the control plane, apply per-request load balancing across the destination's endpoints — which is what fixes HTTP/2 pinning without any client change (Item 114) — and emit consistent metrics and traces without the application knowing. Ambient mode splits this: a per-node component handles mTLS and L4, and an optional per-namespace proxy is added only for workloads that need L7 policy, so the cost is paid only where the features are used.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

When is a mesh worth its complexity?

📍 Seen in the wild: the standard closing question on any platform design that puts "service mesh" on the diagram.

🎯 Really testing: whether you have a threshold, or whether a mesh is a reflex.

The honest threshold has three parts. Language heterogeneity: if every service is Go, one well-maintained library gives you retries, mTLS and metrics with no proxy hop, and a mesh is solving a problem you do not have. Three or more languages and the library approach becomes three implementations drifting apart. Scale of the estate: below roughly a dozen services, the policy surface is small enough to manage explicitly, and the control plane costs more attention than it saves. A hard requirement you cannot meet otherwise — mTLS everywhere for compliance, or per-request balancing of internal gRPC — which is often the real reason and is worth stating as such.

The costs deserve equal airtime. Every internal call gains proxy hops, typically sub-millisecond but non-zero and doubled on the round trip. Every pod gains a proxy's memory and CPU, which at a thousand pods is a real fleet-sized line item — the main motivation for ambient mode. Debugging changes character: a connection failure now has four possible owners instead of two, and reading a request path requires understanding the proxy's config as well as your own. And the control plane becomes a component whose outage degrades certificate rotation and config propagation across everything.

My position: adopt a mesh when you need mTLS across a polyglot estate, or when internal gRPC balancing is already hurting, and adopt it in ambient mode if the platform supports it. Do not adopt it for observability alone — that is the cheapest thing to get another way.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Sidecar mesh Ambient / sidecarless Client library Central L7 tier
Where policy runs A proxy per pod Per node, plus per-namespace for L7 In the application One shared hop
Language independence Yes Yes No — one per language Yes
Per-pod overhead A full proxy None at L4; shared at L7 Library memory only None
Blast radius One pod One node One service The whole tier
Latency added Two proxy hops per call One or two, depending on L7 use None One hop, plus a hairpin
When you'd actually pick it Polyglot estate needing full L7 policy everywhere Same, at scale where per-pod cost hurts Homogeneous estate, one language North–south traffic; the wrong tool for east–west

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The overhead math is what decides adoption at scale. Two proxy hops per call at a few hundred microseconds each is negligible against a 40ms backend, and meaningful against a 2ms internal cache lookup — so the cost lands hardest on the chattiest, fastest calls, which is the opposite of intuition. For a request that fans out to five internal services, ten proxy traversals accumulate, and tail-latency amplification applies: if each hop has a p99 well above its p50, the probability that no hop is slow falls as p^n, so the fan-out's p99 degrades faster than any single hop's.

The resource math is simpler and usually decisive. A sidecar's baseline memory footprint multiplied by pod count is the number that motivated ambient mode: at a thousand pods, per-pod proxies become a fleet-sized cost for a feature most of those pods use only at L4. Ambient's split — a shared per-node L4 component plus an opt-in L7 proxy per namespace — exists to make that bill proportional to the features actually used.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Not for a small, single-language estate. One good library gives you the same behaviour with no hop, no control plane and no new failure mode. A mesh here is complexity with no corresponding requirement.

  • Not for north–south traffic. A mesh handles east–west; external ingress belongs to a gateway or ingress controller, and routing outside traffic through the mesh's internal machinery confuses two different policy problems.

  • Not for observability alone. Distributed tracing and RED metrics are available from libraries, an ingress tier or eBPF-based tooling without putting a proxy in every request path.

  • Not on latency-critical, high-frequency internal calls without measuring first. Two proxy hops on a 2ms call is a double-digit percentage regression, and it will be blamed on the application for weeks.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A service mesh gives you zero-trust security."

✅ Reality: It gives you mTLS and workload identity — transport authentication between services. Authorisation policy, secret management, supply-chain integrity and human access are all still yours to solve. Encrypted traffic between two services that should not be talking is still traffic that should not be happening.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "The sidecar is transparent to the application."

✅ Reality: Transparent to the code, not to the system. Startup ordering matters — an app that dials out before the sidecar is ready fails in ways that look like DNS problems; shutdown ordering matters just as much, since a sidecar that exits first strands in-flight requests; and timeouts now exist in two places, so an application timeout longer than the proxy's means the proxy's is the one that fires.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 113-outlier-detection-circuit-breaking.md — the policies a mesh makes uniform

  • 114-grpc-http2-load-balancing.md — the problem a mesh solves without touching client code

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • 117-ingress-controllers.md — where north–south meets the mesh's east–west

  • 05-tls/ mTLS notes — the identity model underneath

  • 13-kubernetes-networking/ CNI notes — how the interception is actually installed

headings.text: Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)
Walk me through a cache miss at the edge.
Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)
Short TTL with revalidation, or long TTL with explicit purge?
⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)
⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Cache semantics the edge must honour — RFC 9111: HTTP Caching

  • Cache keys and what purging actually invalidates — Cloudflare: Purge cache

  • Edge and browser TTL, and how they interact — Cloudflare: Edge and Browser Cache TTL

  • Bonus — cloudflare.com/learning: Common CDN issues

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What makes a cached object unique? The cache key — by default host + path + query, extended by whatever Vary names.
Two ways to invalidate? Purge (explicit, seconds) or TTL expiry (implicit, up to the TTL). Versioned URLs avoid both.
What does stale-while-revalidate buy? Serve the stale copy instantly and refresh in the background — hides origin latency and outages.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A CDN is a globally distributed reverse-proxy tier: hundreds of points of presence, anycast so clients reach the nearest, and a cache at each one. It shortens the network path — the biggest single latency win available for static content — and it shields the origin, because a cached response never reaches you. Everything interesting is about the cache key and invalidation: what makes two requests "the same object", and how you get a wrong object out of hundreds of caches. Edge compute extends this by running code at the PoP, which is how personalised responses stay cacheable.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Walk me through a cache miss at the edge.

The client's DNS resolves to an anycast address, so the TCP and TLS handshake terminate at the nearest PoP — often 5–20ms away instead of 100ms+ to origin, which is a real saving before any caching happens. The edge computes the cache key from host, path, query string and whatever headers the configuration or the response's Vary says participate, and looks it up.

On a miss, most CDNs do not go straight to origin. They check a mid-tier or shielding layer first, so that a hundred PoPs missing the same object produce one origin request rather than a hundred — that shielding is what turns a cold cache from an origin stampede into a single fetch. The origin's response is stored according to Cache-Control, then returned. Subsequent requests at that PoP are hits; requests at other PoPs are still misses until they fetch it too, which is why CDN hit ratios are per-PoP and why long-tail content caches poorly.

The two headers that determine correctness are Cache-Control — whether it may be cached, by whom, and for how long — and Vary, which adds request headers to the key. A response that varies by user and omits both is the classic edge data-leak: the first user's response is served to everyone else at that PoP.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Short TTL with revalidation, or long TTL with explicit purge?

🎯 Really testing: whether you know that purge is a distributed-systems problem and TTL is not.

Short TTLs are self-correcting: nothing is ever very stale, no coordination is needed, and a mistake ages out on its own. The cost is origin load — every TTL expiry across every PoP produces a revalidation, so a 60-second TTL on a popular object with two hundred PoPs is a steady trickle of origin traffic that never stops, and a conditional request still costs a round trip even when it returns 304.

Long TTLs with purge give you near-zero origin load and immediate invalidation when you need it — modern CDNs propagate a purge globally in well under a second. The cost is that purge is a distributed operation that can fail, be rate limited, or miss variants: purging /page does not purge the Vary-derived variants unless the CDN supports it, and a partial purge leaves some PoPs serving old content with no visible error.

The answer that avoids the choice is versioned URLs — a content hash in the path, cached effectively forever, with a new URL for new content. Nothing is ever invalidated, purge is never needed, and rollback is instant because the old URL still exists. Use immutable URLs for assets, long TTL plus purge for pages you must change on demand, and short TTL only where the object is genuinely time-sensitive and cheap to revalidate. And whichever you pick, stale-while-revalidate should be on: it decouples user-visible latency from origin latency and converts an origin outage into staleness.

4. Quick Comparison Table

Invalidation strategy Staleness window Origin load Failure mode When you'd actually pick it
Short TTL Up to the TTL Continuous revalidation Self-correcting Genuinely time-sensitive, cheap-to-fetch objects
Long TTL + purge Until purge propagates Very low Purge fails silently or misses variants Pages you must change on demand
Versioned / immutable URLs None — the URL changes Minimal None; old versions simply persist Static assets; the default for anything hashable
stale-while-revalidate Bounded, invisible to the user Background only Serves stale during an origin outage — usually a feature Layer it on top of any of the above

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic that justifies a CDN has two independent terms. Path shortening is unconditional: terminating TLS 8ms away instead of 100ms away removes two round trips' worth of distance from every connection, cached or not, which is why CDNs help dynamic content too. Origin offload scales with hit ratio: at hit ratio h, origin traffic is (1 − h) of total, so 95% becomes a twentyfold reduction and 99% a hundredfold. The gap between 95% and 99% is a factor of five in origin fleet size — which is why cache-key hygiene is a capacity decision, not a tuning detail.

Cache-key cardinality is where hit ratio is usually lost. Every value that participates in the key multiplies the number of stored objects: adding a Vary: Accept-Language with twelve locales divides your effective per-object hit ratio across twelve entries, and an unnormalised query string with tracking parameters can turn one object into thousands. The first thing to check on a disappointing hit ratio is always the key, not the TTL.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not cache personalised responses without an explicit key or private. A response that differs by user and is cacheable by default is a data leak across every client hitting that PoP — a correctness failure, not a performance one.

  • Do not put a caching CDN in front of a streaming endpoint without an explicit bypass. A CDN that buffers to store a response destroys time-to-first-token exactly like a buffering reverse proxy (Item 121), and the streaming path is never cacheable anyway.

  • Do not rely on purge as a routine correctness mechanism. It is a distributed operation with rate limits and variant blind spots; if correctness depends on it succeeding everywhere, use versioned URLs instead.

  • Do not treat the CDN as outside your failure domain. It is a shared reverse-proxy tier — the 2021 Fastly outage and the recurring configuration-driven CDN incidents are reminders that this hop can take you offline while every one of your own systems is healthy.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "A CDN only helps static content."

✅ Reality: Path shortening helps every request. Terminating TLS at a nearby PoP and reusing a warm connection to origin removes round trips from uncacheable, fully dynamic requests too — which is why "dynamic acceleration" is a real product rather than marketing.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "Cache hit ratio is mostly about TTL length."

✅ Reality: It is mostly about the cache key. Unnormalised query strings, an over-broad Vary, and per-request cookies fragment one object into many, and no TTL fixes a key that never repeats. Normalising the key routinely buys more than doubling the TTL.

18. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first to understand this concept)

  • 105-reverse-proxy-responsibilities.md — a CDN is that responsibility list, distributed

  • 07-http-semantics/62-http-caching.md — the freshness and Vary semantics the edge implements

  • 115-global-load-balancing.md — anycast, which is how clients find the nearest PoP

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen this concept)

  • breadth.md — WAF and DDoS mitigation, which live at the same hop

  • 121-buffering-vs-streaming-proxies.md — why the streaming path must bypass this tier

  • 04-dns/32-ttl-and-caching-layers.md — the other caching hierarchy that shapes what clients see

notes.title: WAF, DDoS Protection & Bot Mitigation

headings.text: 📚 Reference Links
1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)
2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • What a WAF inspects and where it sits — Cloudflare Learning: What is a WAF?

  • Attack shapes and where each is absorbed — Cloudflare Learning: What is a DDoS attack?

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where does a WAF sit? At an L7 hop, after TLS termination — it must read the request to inspect it.
Volumetric vs application-layer DDoS? Volumetric floods the pipe (absorbed at the edge by capacity); L7 floods expensive endpoints with valid-looking requests.
Why is bot mitigation not just rate limiting? Distributed bots stay under any per-IP limit; detection uses fingerprints, behaviour and challenges instead.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

These three sit at the outermost L7 hop — CDN edge or the load balancer — and each handles a different attack shape. A WAF inspects decrypted requests against rules for injection, traversal and known exploit patterns, and can block or challenge. DDoS protection is mostly capacity and anycast: volumetric floods are absorbed by spreading them across every PoP, while application-layer floods need rate limiting and challenges because the requests look legitimate. Bot mitigation separates automated clients from humans using fingerprints, behavioural signals and challenges, since a distributed botnet never trips a per-IP limit. All three require TLS termination, which is why they cannot exist on an L4 pass-through path — and all three trade false positives against coverage, so the operational reality is a tuning window in monitor-only mode before anything is set to block.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The default that causes this, and the directives that fix it — nginx: ngx_http_proxy_module

  • The wire format being broken — MDN: Using server-sent events

  • Where to set it per-route in Kubernetes — Kubernetes: Ingress

  • The idle timeout that cuts long streams — AWS: Edit attributes for your Application Load Balancer

  • Bonus — Envoy: Life of a Request

1. 🎯 Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What is nginx's proxy_buffering default? on — the response is held until a buffer fills or the upstream closes.
Which origin header disables it without touching config? X-Accel-Buffering: no, sent by the backend.
Which three settings break streaming together? Response buffering, compression (gzip re-buffers), and a short idle/read timeout.
What is the symptom, precisely? TTFB equals full response time. Zero errors, all health checks green.
Why doesn't curl reproduce it against the app? You bypassed the proxy. The bug lives in the hop, so you must curl through it.

🪞 How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read the note. Second pass — re-test only the misses. Third pass (day before) — full re-test.

2. Tech Discussion Explanation (30 Seconds)

A buffering proxy reads the whole upstream response before sending any of it to the client, which is right for a document and catastrophic for a stream. nginx buffers by default, so an SSE token stream that the backend emits over eight seconds arrives at the browser as one blob at the eight-second mark — time-to-first-token goes from 200 milliseconds to eight seconds. Nothing errors, every health check passes, and curl against the app directly looks perfect because it skips the hop. The fixes are proxy_buffering off, gzip off on that route, and a read timeout longer than the stream.

3. Deep Tech Discussion Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification (senior engineer testing if you know the basics)

Why does a proxy buffer at all, if it hurts this much?

🎯 Really testing: whether you can defend the default rather than just disable it.

Buffering protects the upstream from slow clients. If the proxy relays byte-for-byte, a client on a poor mobile connection holds an application worker or connection open for the whole duration of the transfer — the classic slowloris shape, where a handful of deliberately slow readers exhaust a backend's connection pool. By reading the response as fast as the backend can produce it and then dribbling it out at the client's pace, the proxy frees the expensive resource immediately and absorbs the slowness itself. That is a genuinely good trade for a 200KB JSON document.

It also enables things that need the whole body: computing Content-Length instead of chunking, compressing efficiently, and retrying a failed upstream request on another backend — which a proxy can only do if it has not already sent part of the response to the client. Once the first byte leaves, the response is committed and no retry is possible.

For a stream, every one of those benefits inverts. There is no "whole body" — the response is unbounded by design; Content-Length is unknowable; compression is a latency tax; and the point of the exchange is that bytes arrive as they are produced. Buffering does not merely fail to help, it destroys the only property that mattered.

Tier 2 — Trade-off (senior engineer testing your judgement)

Should you disable buffering globally or per route?

📍 Seen in the wild: the follow-up after "we turned buffering off and it fixed it".

🎯 Really testing: whether you understand what you give up when you turn it off, or whether you have learned one directive.

Per route, always — because the setting is correct on one and wrong on the other, and a global switch is choosing to be wrong somewhere. With buffering off globally, every slow-client transfer now pins an upstream connection for its full duration, so a fleet sized for buffered behaviour discovers a concurrency ceiling it did not have; upstream retries stop working, because the proxy has already committed bytes to the client; and responses lose Content-Length, which some clients and intermediaries handle worse than others.

The counter-consideration is operational: two configurations mean two behaviours to reason about, and the streaming route is the one that gets forgotten when someone adds a new endpoint. Mitigate that with an explicit convention — a path prefix like /stream/ or a route annotation applied by template — rather than by making the wrong setting global.

There is a middle option worth naming: have the backend send X-Accel-Buffering: no on streaming responses. That moves the decision to the code that knows whether a response is a stream, works without a proxy config change, and travels with the endpoint when it moves. Its limitation is that only nginx-family proxies honour it, so it complements route config rather than replacing it.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling (senior engineer testing depth)

You disable buffering for 20,000 concurrent SSE streams. What breaks?

📍 Seen in the wild: the capacity follow-up on any streaming product.

Upstream connection count, because buffering was what decoupled it from client count. With buffering on, the proxy can finish reading from the backend and release that connection while it slowly feeds the client — so upstream concurrency tracks backend speed. With it off, each client connection pins one upstream connection for the full life of the stream, so 20,000 streams is 20,000 upstream connections plus 20,000 client connections: 40,000 sockets on the proxy and 20,000 workers or async tasks on the backend. A backend that comfortably served 20,000 buffered requests per minute may not survive 20,000 simultaneous open streams.

It presents as a ceiling, not a slope: below the limit everything is fine, and at the limit new connections are accepted and immediately reset while CPU sits idle. The signals are worker_connections are not enough in the nginx error log, accept() failures, a listen backlog at somaxconn, and upstream connection counts pinned at whatever worker_connections allows. The remedies are raising file-descriptor and worker-connection limits on both sides, running the streaming routes on their own proxy pool so a ceiling there cannot take down normal traffic, and — the structural fix — moving fan-out to a layer designed for it, so one upstream stream can serve many clients rather than one each.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design the full delivery path for LLM token streaming, browser to model, so that time-to-first-token survives every hop.

📍 Seen in the wild: the AI-product form of this note; the reason it is tagged [C].

🎯 Really testing: whether you audit every hop rather than fixing the one you know about.

The dominating constraint is that time-to-first-token is a product metric, and every hop between the model and the browser can independently destroy it. So the design method is an audit, not a fix: list the hops, and for each one name its buffering behaviour, its compression behaviour and its idle timeout. A typical path is browser → CDN → cloud load balancer → ingress controller → application → model server, which is five opportunities to buffer and five idle timeouts to exceed.

Concretely: the CDN must bypass cache and buffering for the streaming path — most edges do not buffer chunked responses, but the streaming route should be explicitly excluded from caching and from any transform. The cloud balancer needs its idle timeout raised well beyond the longest expected generation, since an ALB's 60-second default silently cuts long responses mid-stream. The ingress controller needs buffering and gzip off for that route, which in an NGINX ingress is an annotation and in a Gateway API implementation a route-level setting. The application must flush per token rather than relying on the framework's default buffered writer — a framework-level StreamingResponse that still buffers is a common late discovery. And the model server must emit incrementally, which is its default but is defeated by any middleware that collects the generator.

The failure I would monitor first is TTFB on the streaming route specifically, measured at the client, not at the server. Server-side latency looks identical whether or not a proxy buffered — the backend emitted its first token in 200ms either way — so only client-side or synthetic measurement detects it. Second is a canary that asserts an inter-chunk gap: a synthetic request that fails if the second chunk arrives less than a chosen interval after the first, which catches "the response was correct but arrived all at once". That assertion is the only reliable regression test for this bug, and it belongs in CI, because the failure will be reintroduced by an unrelated config change.

6. Mechanism & Math (How It Actually Works)

The arithmetic of the damage. Perceived latency for a streamed response is time-to-first-token; for a buffered one it is total generation time. With a 200ms TTFT and 40 tokens per second over 320 tokens, the stream feels instant and completes in 8 seconds, while the buffered version is a blank screen for 8 seconds — a 40× regression in the number users actually perceive, with identical server-side latency metrics. That ratio, total_time / TTFT, is the size of the bug and it grows with response length: longer generations are hurt more, so the failure gets worse exactly as the product gets more capable.

Why the buffer size does not save you. nginx's proxy_buffers default is 8 buffers of 4k or one page each. A response is released early only if it exceeds the buffer capacity — so a short stream of a few hundred bytes per second may never fill 32KB and is held until the upstream closes. Counter-intuitively, large responses partially escape the bug while small ones are fully trapped, which is why the problem often survives testing with long prompts and appears with short ones.

Compression re-imposes it. gzip operates on blocks; a compressor that flushes per chunk produces poor ratios, so implementations buffer. Turning proxy_buffering off while leaving gzip on for that route reintroduces the identical symptom one layer up, which is the most common half-fix.

Idle timeouts are the second, independent failure. A stream that emits a token every few seconds is active to the application and idle to any hop measuring gaps between bytes. An ALB's 60-second default idle timeout and nginx's 60-second proxy_read_timeout both fire on the gap, not on the total, so a long generation with a slow section is cut mid-response and the client receives a truncated body with a 200 status — no error anywhere.

7. Why It Matters in Production

This is the highest-frequency, lowest-visibility bug in the whole section, and it has become more common because every product now streams. It produces no errors, no failed health checks, no 5xx, and no server-side latency change — the entire signal is client-side, on a metric most teams add only after they have been bitten.

The observable is client-measured time-to-first-token, and its diagnostic partner is the ratio of client TTFB to server TTFB. When those two diverge by an order of magnitude, a hop between them is buffering; when they track each other, the latency is real. No amount of application profiling finds this, because the application is innocent.

The business framing is worth having ready: streaming exists entirely to make a slow operation feel fast. A buffered stream delivers the same bytes with the same server cost and none of the perceived-speed benefit, which means the feature has been paid for and switched off by a default in a config file.

8. Command / Config / Code Example

location /v1/chat/stream {
  proxy_pass http://app_pool;
  proxy_http_version 1.1;        # 1.0 default breaks chunked transfer entirely
  proxy_buffering off;           # THE fix - deliver chunks as they arrive
  proxy_cache off;               # caching implies collecting the whole body
  gzip off;                      # compression re-buffers what we just unbuffered
  proxy_read_timeout 3600s;      # gap between reads, not total - a long stream is not idle
  proxy_set_header Connection "";        # keep the upstream keepalive pool usable
  chunked_transfer_encoding on;
}

# The application half: flush per token, and tell nginx-family proxies not to buffer
@app.get("/v1/chat/stream")
async def stream(prompt: str):
    async def gen():
        async for token in model.generate(prompt):
            yield f"data: {token}\n\n"        # SSE frame, flushed per token
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream",
        headers={"X-Accel-Buffering": "no",  # honoured by nginx without config access
                 "Cache-Control": "no-cache"})

# The test that actually proves it - note the timestamps, and the URL through the PROXY
curl -N --no-buffer https://api.example.com/v1/chat/stream?prompt=hi \
  | while IFS= read -r line; do printf '%s %s\n' "$(date +%T.%3N)" "$line"; done

10. When TO Use This

(Read as: when buffering is the correct setting.)

  • Keep buffering on for ordinary request/response traffic. It protects backends from slow clients, frees upstream connections early, and is the reason a modest fleet can serve clients on poor networks.

  • Keep it on where upstream retries matter. A proxy can only retry a request on another backend if it has not yet committed bytes to the client; buffering is what preserves that option.

  • Keep it on for large downloads to slow clients. This is the case buffering was designed for, and turning it off converts every slow reader into a pinned backend worker.

  • Turn it off, per route, for anything the client consumes incrementally — SSE, chunked JSON lines, long-poll responses, log tailing, progress endpoints.

11. ⚠️ When NOT To Use This

  • Do not disable buffering globally to fix one route. You inherit the slowloris exposure and lose upstream retries across the whole service to fix an endpoint that could have been configured on its own.

  • Do not disable buffering and leave compression on. gzip buffers by nature; the symptom returns unchanged and the next person concludes that buffering was not the problem.

  • Do not stream without auditing every hop's idle timeout. Buffering and idle timeouts are two independent failures with the same-shaped symptom; fixing one and not the other converts "arrives all at once" into "arrives incrementally and then stops".

  • Do not assume Envoy-based paths are safe. Envoy streams by default, but a buffer filter added for a different route, or an ingress annotation applied at the wrong scope, reintroduces it — and the Envoy version of this bug is harder to spot because the default was fine.

  • Scale limit worth naming: unbuffered streaming pins one upstream connection per client for the stream's whole life, so concurrency is bounded by file descriptors and backend workers rather than by throughput. Plan the fan-out layer before you plan the proxy config.

12. Common Misconceptions

❌ Misconception: "The backend is slow — look at the model server."

✅ Reality: Server-side TTFB is unchanged; only client-side TTFB moved. Comparing the two is a two-minute check that redirects the entire investigation, and skipping it is how teams spend days profiling a generation path that was never the problem.

❌ Misconception: "proxy_buffering off is the whole fix."

✅ Reality: It is one of at least four settings on one of at least four hops. Compression, cache, read timeouts and the application's own response writer each reproduce the same symptom independently, and the CDN and cloud balancer have their own versions.

🪞 Personal misconception (held before learning): "If curl streams correctly, streaming works."

✅ Reality: Only if you curl the public URL, through every hop, with -N. curl against the app's internal address skips the proxy that has the bug, and curl without -N buffers on the client side, so the test can fail in two independent ways while the server is fine.

13. Tech Discussion Traps

Naming the directive without naming the mechanism. "Set proxy_buffering off" is a fix you memorised. "The proxy reads the whole upstream response before forwarding, so time-to-first-byte becomes total response time — which is exactly the property streaming exists to provide" is an explanation, and it generalises to the CDN, the compressor and the framework's response writer.

Not defending the default. A senior reviewer will ask why buffering exists at all, and an answer that treats it as a mistake fails. Slow-client protection and retry preservation are real, which is why the fix is per-route rather than global.

Ignoring the middle of the path. People fix nginx and stop. The CDN, the cloud balancer, the ingress annotation scope and the framework's writer are four more places with the same failure, and a design answer that audits one hop has audited the one it happened to know about.

Confusing buffering with timeouts. Both produce broken streams, and they need opposite fixes. Buffering delays the first byte; an idle timeout truncates a stream that started fine. Distinguishing them by the timestamp signature — everything at the end, versus fine then stopping — is the mark of having debugged it rather than read about it.

Quoting a latency number with no source. "It adds some latency" understates it by an order of magnitude. The defensible form is the ratio: total generation time over TTFT, which for a typical response is 30–50×, and which you can measure in one curl.

16. Real World Usage

Every LLM product ships a version of this configuration. The two-location-block pattern — normal defaults on the API routes, buffering and compression off with a long read timeout on the streaming route — is the standard shape of a production config for a chat product, not a teaching example.

The Kubernetes ecosystem has a dedicated annotation for it. nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off" exists because the failure is common enough to need a per-Ingress override, and the equivalent surfaces as first-class route configuration under the Gateway API — a good indication of how often this bites.

It is the most common cause of "our streaming is broken in production but fine locally". Local development runs the app directly with no proxy; staging often has a simpler ingress than production; and the CDN usually exists only in production. Each of those gaps hides the bug until the environment that has all the hops is the one in front of users.

19. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design tech discussion

It arrives inside an AI-product design, usually as "the demo streams, production doesn't — what would you check?" The strong answer treats it as a path audit rather than a single fix: enumerate the hops, name each one's buffering, compression and idle-timeout behaviour, and identify which metric would have caught it. The follow-up is nearly always capacity — what unbuffered streaming does to connection counts — which is where the design conversation actually lives.

Topology diagram

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10× (5k concurrent streams) 10k sockets on the proxy; backend workers held for stream duration Raise worker_connections and ulimit -n; async backend so a stream is a task, not a thread
100× (50k streams) Proxy memory and per-connection state; a single proxy is now a large blast radius Dedicated streaming proxy pool, separate from request/response traffic; horizontal scale
1000× (500k streams) Connection-per-client to the model tier is untenable; egress bytes dominate Fan-out layer between app and model so one generation can serve many subscribers; regional streaming tiers

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • 10×: file descriptors and worker connections. A cliff, not a slope — resets while CPU is idle.

  • 100×: backend concurrency. Streams are long-lived, so a fleet sized on requests-per-second is sized on the wrong unit entirely.

  • Operational: a config change on an unrelated route reintroduces buffering or compression at one hop, and nothing alerts because the status codes are all 200.

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Client-measured time-to-first-token, p50 and p99, on the streaming route only. Server-side latency cannot see this failure at all.

  • Ratio of client TTFB to server TTFB, alerting above ~3. The direct detector; it names a buffering hop without any other instrumentation.

  • A synthetic canary asserting an inter-chunk gap. Fails if the second chunk arrives with the first — the only reliable regression test, and it belongs in CI as well as in production monitoring.

  • Concurrent stream count against the proxy's connection ceiling, as a ratio. Alert at 70%, because past 100% the failure is a reset cliff rather than a slowdown.
